rv.summary: Sociology studies religion empirically, comparatively and without judging which faith is true, unlike theology. Religions share beliefs and rituals, sacred symbols and a community of believers; Durkheim separated the sacred from the profane. Religion links with power and stratification.
remember: Sociological study of religion: empirical, comparative, non-judgemental
Features: shared beliefs and rituals, sacred symbols, community of believers
Durkheim: sacred = set apart with awe and reverence; profane = ordinary everyday world
traps: Sociologists do not decide which religion is true
Comparison does not mean ranking religions

topics.h: Why did modern capitalism first flourish in certain parts of Protestant Europe? Max Weber found a surprising answer in religious ideas.
p: Max Weber, in The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism, argued that the Calvinist ethic of hard work, discipline and frugality contributed to the rise of capitalism: wealth was reinvested rather than spent on luxury.
Religion is linked with gender: religious norms often shape women's roles, and religious reform has also been used to question gender inequality.
Religion can promote social change: e.g. Bhakti saints and modern reform movements challenged caste hierarchy and ritualism.

Secularisation thesis: modern societies were expected to become less religious. Yet religion remains publicly important in many societies, including India, and religious identity often figures in public life.

ex.q: Explain Weber's argument linking Calvinism to capitalism in three steps.
st: Calvinists valued hard work in one's calling as a religious duty.
They rejected luxury and practised frugality, so they saved.
Savings were reinvested in business, encouraging capitalist growth.
ex.a: A religious ethic of disciplined work and frugality encouraged saving and reinvestment, helping capitalism grow.

topics.rl: Bhakti saints like Kabir and Ravidas used vernacular poetry to question caste and ritual; their verses are still sung across north India, showing religion as a source of social change.

rv.summary: Weber argued that the Calvinist ethic of hard work and frugality helped capitalism grow, as wealth was reinvested rather than spent. Religion shapes gender roles and can drive change, as Bhakti saints challenged caste.
focus: The secularisation thesis and its limits
remember: Weber: Calvinist work ethic and frugality → saving and reinvestment → capitalism
Bhakti saints and reform movements challenged caste hierarchy and ritualism
Secularisation thesis: religion expected to decline with modernity
traps: Weber did not say capitalism destroyed religion
The secularisation thesis is not the same as a secular state

topics.h: At home you are 'Chintu', the family's darling. At school you are Roll No. 23, judged by the same rules as everyone else. That shift is a big lesson in itself.
p: Education is a lifelong process of learning; schooling is its formal, institutionalised form (with set curricula, teachers and certificates).
Emile Durkheim saw education as transmitting society's shared norms and values, creating the common bonds a society needs to survive.
In simple societies, children learn through daily community life; complex societies need formal schooling because knowledge and skills are specialised.
Schools teach universalistic values (the same rules and standards for everyone) in contrast to the particularistic values of the family (treating a person as special because of a relationship).

ex.q: Show the difference between particularistic and universalistic values using exam marks.
st: At home: parents may excuse low marks because 'you are our child' (particularistic).
At school: every answer sheet is marked on the same scheme regardless of who you are (universalistic).
School thus prepares children for a society governed by impersonal, common rules.
ex.a: Families judge by relationship (particularistic); schools apply the same standards to all (universalistic).

topics.rl: CBSE board exams use roll numbers and a common marking scheme for lakhs of students, a clear example of universalistic standards.

rv.summary: Education is lifelong learning; schooling is its formal part. Durkheim saw education as transmitting society's shared norms and values. Simple societies teach through daily life, complex ones need schools, which apply universalistic values unlike the family's particularistic ones.
remember: Schooling: formal, institutionalised education with curricula, teachers, certificates
Durkheim: education transmits shared norms and values, creating social bonds
Universalistic: same rules for everyone (school); particularistic: special treatment by relationship (family)
traps: Schools teach values, not only the syllabus
Particularistic values belong to families, not courts or exams

topics.h: Two Class 10 students: one in an international school with a robotics lab, another in a village school with one teacher for three classes. Same exam, different starting lines.
p: Functionalist view: education prepares people for adult roles and allocates them to occupations according to merit.
Conflict view: education reproduces social inequality. Elite private schools and under-resourced schools prepare children for very different futures.
The hidden curriculum: values and norms taught implicitly, e.g. obedience, gender roles, or a sense of who is 'meant' to succeed.
Access is unequal by class, caste and gender: e.g. dropout rates have historically been higher among girls from Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes.
Exam skill: discuss religion and education as social institutions with examples.

ex.q: Apply both views to the fact that most toppers of an entrance exam come from expensive coaching.
st: Functionalist: the exam sorts students by merit into suitable occupations.
Conflict: costly coaching is affordable mainly to richer families, so the exam rewards class advantage.
Hidden curriculum: students learn that success 'belongs' to some groups.
ex.a: Functionalists see merit-based sorting; conflict theorists see class advantage reproduced through education.

topics.rl: The Right to Education Act, 2009 reserves 25% of entry-level seats in private unaided schools for children from disadvantaged groups, an attempt to reduce educational inequality.

rv.summary: Functionalists say education prepares people for adult roles and allocates jobs by merit; conflict theorists say it reproduces inequality, as elite and poor schools give different futures. The hidden curriculum teaches norms implicitly, and access is unequal by class, caste and gender.
focus: Functionalist vs conflict views of education
remember: Functionalist: education prepares for adult roles and allocates by merit
Conflict: education reproduces social inequality
Hidden curriculum: implicit values like obedience and gender roles
traps: The hidden curriculum is not secret exam papers
Equal exams do not mean equal starting points

topics.t: Culture as a map; culture in everyday versus sociological sense
topics.h: Someone says 'She is very cultured' because she loves classical music. A sociologist would say the street-food vendor and the tribal farmer are just as 'cultured'. Who is right?
p: Culture works like a map or toolkit: shared ways of thinking, behaving and interpreting the world that guide us through social life.
Culture is learned (not inborn), shared by members of a group, and always changing.
Cultures cannot be ranked as superior or inferior; they are judged by how adequate they are for their own settings.
In everyday use, 'culture' often means 'high culture' (classical arts, refined taste). Sociologically, culture is the whole way of life of a people.
Socialisation is the process by which we learn culture and become social beings.

ex.q: Explain how the sociological meaning of 'culture' differs from saying 'Riya is cultured because she learns Bharatanatyam'.
st: Everyday sense: culture = high arts and refinement, so some people 'have more'.
Sociological sense: culture = entire learned, shared way of life (food, language, beliefs, tools, dance, festivals).
So everyone has culture; Riya's dance is one part of her culture, not proof of having 'more'.
ex.a: Sociologically everyone has culture: it is the whole learned, shared way of life, not only the fine arts.

topics.rl: Mumbai's dabbawalas run a complex lunch-delivery system using shared codes and routines learned on the job, a living example of culture as a toolkit.

rv.summary: Culture is like a map or toolkit: the whole learned, shared and changing way of life of a group, not only 'high culture'. Cultures cannot be ranked; they are judged by how well they suit their settings. Socialisation is how we learn culture.
focus: Sociological vs everyday meaning of culture
remember: Culture: the whole learned and shared way of life of a group
Culture is learned, shared and always changing
Socialisation: the process by which we learn culture
traps: Culture is not only classical arts or refined taste
Culture is not inborn and fixed

topics.h: When the 2004 tsunami struck the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, some indigenous communities read the signs of the sea and moved to high ground in time. Their culture was their early-warning system.
p: Different environments produce different cultures, because people develop knowledge and practices suited to their surroundings.

During the 2004 tsunami, indigenous communities of the Andaman Islands, such as the Onge and Jarawa, are reported to have survived largely by recognising natural warning signs passed down through traditional knowledge.
Culture includes non-verbal communication: gestures, facial expressions and signals that members share and understand.
Shared codes differ across cultures: a head-shake, a namaste or a thumbs-up can mean different things in different places.

ex.q: Why might a gesture that is polite in one place be confusing in another? Use the head-wobble as an example.
st: Gestures are cultural codes, learned not inborn.
In parts of India a side-to-side head movement can mean 'yes' or 'okay'.
A visitor who has learned a different code may read it as 'no' or 'maybe'.
So non-verbal meanings depend on shared culture.
ex.a: Because non-verbal signals are learned shared codes; outsiders without the code may misread them.

topics.rl: Traffic hand signals by Indian police, cricket umpires' signals and the namaste greeting are shared non-verbal codes that everyone in the setting understands.

rv.summary: Different environments produce different cultures, as people build knowledge suited to their surroundings — the Onge and Jarawa read natural signs during the 2004 tsunami. Culture also includes non-verbal communication, and gestures are learned codes that differ across cultures.
remember: Andaman communities like the Onge and Jarawa survived the 2004 tsunami using traditional knowledge
Non-verbal communication: gestures, facial expressions, signals
Gestures are learned shared codes that vary across cultures
traps: Traditional knowledge is not useless in the modern world
Gestures are not inborn or universal

topics.h: Ask three famous anthropologists 'What is culture?' and you get three answers: a complex whole, a toolkit of artefacts and habits, and a web of meanings. Together they give us the full picture.
p: Edward Tylor (1871): culture is that complex whole which includes knowledge, belief, art, morals, law, custom and any other capabilities and habits acquired by humans as members of society.
Bronislaw Malinowski: culture comprises inherited artefacts, goods, technical processes, ideas, habits and values. He pioneered intensive fieldwork in the Trobriand Islands.
Clifford Geertz: humans are suspended in webs of significance they themselves have spun; culture is those webs of meaning through which people interpret their experience.

Other anthropologists, such as A.L. Kroeber and Clyde Kluckhohn, reviewed many definitions, and Leslie White stressed the use of symbols; most agree culture is shared, learned behaviour based on symbols.

ex.q: Which definition fits best: (a) a list of everything a society has, from law to habits; (b) material objects plus ideas; (c) meanings people use to interpret life?
st: (a) 'complex whole' of knowledge, belief, art, morals, law, custom: Tylor.
(b) artefacts, goods, technical processes, ideas, habits, values: Malinowski.
(c) webs of significance/meaning: Geertz.
ex.a: (a) Tylor, (b) Malinowski, (c) Geertz.

topics.rl: Think of Diwali: Tylor would list its beliefs, art and customs; Malinowski would add lamps, sweets and firecracker-making techniques; Geertz would ask what lighting a diya means to a family.

rv.summary: Tylor (1871) called culture a complex whole of knowledge, belief, art, morals, law, custom and habits acquired as members of society. Malinowski, pioneer of Trobriand fieldwork, included artefacts and technical processes; Geertz saw culture as webs of meaning.
focus: Material and non-material elements in Malinowski
remember: Tylor: 'complex whole' — knowledge, belief, art, morals, law, custom, habits
Malinowski: artefacts, goods, technical processes, ideas, habits, values; Trobriand Islands
Geertz: humans suspended in self-spun webs of significance (meaning)
traps: Don't give Geertz's 'webs of meaning' to Tylor or Malinowski
Culture is acquired as a member of society, not inherited biologically

topics.t: Dimensions of culture: cognitive and material; culture lag
topics.h: Smartphones reached villages in a few years, but rules about how to use them politely, safely and privately are still catching up. Sociologists call this a culture lag.
p: Culture has three dimensions: cognitive (how we make sense of information), normative (rules of conduct) and material (tools, technology, objects).

Cognitive dimension: how we learn and arrange information. Oral cultures pass on knowledge through memory, stories and lore; literate cultures record it in books and documents. Literacy and media keep changing how we know.
Material dimension: tools, technology, artefacts, machines and how they are used, e.g. ploughs, phones, the internet.
Culture lag (W.F. Ogburn): non-material culture (norms, values) changes more slowly than material culture (technology), creating a gap.
The dimensions are interrelated: a new tool (material) brings new knowledge (cognitive) and needs new rules (normative).

ex.q: Show how the arrival of UPI payments affected all three dimensions of culture.
st: Material: phones, QR codes, banking apps.
Cognitive: people learn to scan, read balances and understand digital transactions.
Normative: new rules emerge: never share OTPs, confirm before paying; laws on cyber fraud.
Lag: norms on safety often lag behind the speed of the technology, so frauds occur.
ex.a: UPI changed material culture first; cognitive and normative culture had to catch up, illustrating culture lag.

topics.rl: Cyber-fraud cases rose as digital payments spread faster than safe-use habits; RBI awareness campaigns like 'RBI Kehta Hai' try to close this culture lag.

rv.summary: Culture has cognitive (how we know), normative (rules) and material (tools, technology) dimensions, which are interrelated. Oral cultures keep knowledge by memory, literate ones by records. Ogburn's culture lag is when norms change more slowly than technology.
remember: Dimensions: cognitive, normative, material
Material culture: tools, technology, artefacts (e.g. mobile phone)
Culture lag (W.F. Ogburn): non-material culture changes more slowly than material culture
traps: Don't reverse culture lag — it is norms lagging behind technology
The three dimensions are not separate from one another

topics.t: The normative dimension: norms, laws and sanctions
topics.h: Nobody arrests you for not touching an elder's feet, but you might get a look. Skip a red light, though, and you may get a challan. Norms and laws work differently.
p: The normative dimension is made up of rules of conduct: folkways, mores, customs, conventions and laws.

Folkways are everyday conventions (greeting, table manners); mores are norms with strong moral weight (honesty, respecting life); customs are long-established practices; conventions are accepted ways of doing things.
Norms are implicit (often unwritten); laws are explicit, written rules formally enforced by the state.
Norms may vary by status and can discriminate, e.g. norms that restrict women's movement or that once excluded some castes from temples.
Sanctions (rewards and punishments) enforce norms and laws.

ex.q: Classify: (a) eating with your right hand at a family meal, (b) not stealing, (c) the Motor Vehicles Act's helmet rule.
st: (a) Everyday convention, mild disapproval if broken: folkway.
(b) Strong moral rule, serious disapproval: more (plural mores).
(c) Written rule enforced by the state with fines: law.
ex.a: (a) folkway, (b) more, (c) law.

topics.rl: The Prohibition of Child Marriage Act, 2006 turned a long-debated social norm into explicit law: marrying off a girl below 18 or a boy below 21 is now a punishable offence, not just a matter of custom.

rv.summary: The normative dimension is rules of conduct: folkways (everyday conventions), mores (strong moral rules), customs, conventions and laws. Norms are implicit; laws are explicit and enforced by the state. Norms can vary by status and discriminate, and sanctions enforce both.
focus: Folkways, mores, customs, conventions and laws
remember: Folkways: everyday conventions; mores: norms with strong moral weight
Norms are implicit; laws are explicit, written and enforced by the state
Norms may vary by gender, age or caste and can discriminate
traps: Laws are not implicit or unwritten
Mores are not trivial — they carry moral weight

topics.h: At school you are a 'backbencher', at home 'the youngest', at the gym 'the beginner', on Instagram 'the meme queen'. Who you are depends on the roles you play.
p: Identity is not inborn; it is socially formed through the roles we play and the groups we belong to (family, community, school, occupation).
Each role carries shared codes understood by those who play related roles, e.g. how a doctor and patient, or a batter and bowler, are expected to behave.
Sub-cultures are groups within a larger culture that share distinct styles, tastes, language and values, e.g. youth groups, music fans, gamers.
Sub-cultures mark identity and boundaries: they give members a sense of belonging and difference from others.

ex.q: A group of college students who follow K-pop wear similar clothes, use special slang and meet for dance practice. What concepts apply?
st: Distinct style, taste and language within Indian youth culture: a sub-culture.
Shared codes (slang, gestures) understood only by fans.
Members gain identity and belonging from the group.
ex.a: They form a sub-culture that shapes members' identity through shared codes.

topics.rl: Indian hip-hop crews from Mumbai's Dharavi and Delhi's neighbourhoods have built a sub-culture with their own slang, fashion and music, celebrating local identity.

rv.summary: Identity is not inborn; it forms through the roles we play and groups we belong to, each with shared codes. Sub-cultures are groups within a larger culture with distinct styles, tastes, language and values; they give members belonging and difference. 'Sub' means within, not inferior.
remember: Identity is formed through roles and group membership
Sub-culture: group within a larger culture with distinct styles and values (youth groups, music fans, gamers)
Sub-cultures mark identity and boundaries
traps: 'Sub-culture' does not mean an inferior culture
Identity is not fixed at birth

topics.h: In 1835, Thomas Macaulay claimed that a single shelf of a good European library was worth the whole native literature of India and Arabia. That is ethnocentrism in its purest form.
p: Ethnocentrism: judging other cultures by the standards of one's own, which is assumed to be superior.
It often arises when cultures come into contact, as in colonial attitudes. Macaulay's Minute on Indian Education (1835) dismissed Indian learning as inferior to European knowledge.
Cosmopolitanism: valuing other cultures and openly borrowing from them, without insisting on one's own superiority.
Examples of cultural borrowing: English has absorbed words like 'bungalow', 'pyjama' and 'jungle'; Hindi film music blends many styles; Hinglish mixes Hindi and English.
Cosmopolitanism suits modern societies because of migration, media and trade, which bring constant contact between cultures.

ex.q: Classify: (a) 'Our food is the only proper food; others eat strange things.' (b) 'Let's try the Kashmiri wazwan and learn how it is made.'
st: (a) Judges others by one's own standards, assumes superiority: ethnocentrism.
(b) Values and borrows from another culture: cosmopolitanism.
ex.a: (a) ethnocentrism; (b) cosmopolitanism.

topics.rl: Bollywood songs mixing Punjabi folk beats, Arabic melodies and Western pop, and the global spread of yoga, are everyday cosmopolitanism.

rv.summary: Ethnocentrism judges other cultures by one's own standards, assumed superior, often arising from contact — as in Macaulay's 1835 Minute dismissing Indian learning. Cosmopolitanism values and borrows from other cultures, seen in words like 'bungalow' and 'pyjama', and suits modern societies.
remember: Ethnocentrism: judging other cultures by one's own standards
Macaulay's Minute on Indian Education, 1835: colonial ethnocentrism
Cosmopolitanism: valuing and openly borrowing from other cultures
traps: Ethnocentrism is not careful study of one's own culture
Cosmopolitanism does not simply mean living in a big city

topics.h: Jeans replacing dhotis took decades. The French Revolution swept away a king in a few years. Cultures change both slowly and suddenly.
p: Cultural change can come from internal causes (new ideas, inventions, reform within a society) and external causes (contact with other cultures, conquest, trade).
Natural or ecological change, such as deforestation, drought or floods, can force changes in a community's way of life, e.g. forest-dependent communities losing forest-based practices.
Evolutionary change is slow and gradual; revolutionary change is rapid and sweeping.
The French Revolution (1789) is a classic example of revolutionary change, which transformed ideas of monarchy, rights and citizenship.
Exam skill: compare evolutionary and revolutionary approaches to cultural change, with examples.

ex.q: Classify: (a) the gradual shift from joint to nuclear families in some cities; (b) the French Revolution; (c) changes in a tribe's life after its forest is cleared for a dam.
st: (a) slow, over decades: evolutionary, internal and economic causes.
(b) sudden overthrow of monarchy: revolutionary.
(c) ecological change forcing a new way of life (natural/ecological cause).
ex.a: (a) evolutionary; (b) revolutionary; (c) change caused by ecological disruption.

topics.rl: Television and then smartphones reached Indian villages within a generation, changing everyday language, fashion and aspirations; an example of external, technology-driven change.

rv.summary: Cultural change has internal causes (inventions, reform) and external causes (contact, conquest, trade), and ecological change like deforestation can also force it. Evolutionary change is slow and gradual; revolutionary change, like the French Revolution of 1789, is rapid and sweeping.
focus: Internal vs external causes of change
remember: Internal causes: new ideas, inventions, reform; external: contact, conquest, trade
Evolutionary: slow, gradual; revolutionary: rapid, sweeping
French Revolution (1789): classic revolutionary change
traps: Not all cultural change is slow
Conquest and colonial rule are external, not internal, causes

topics.h: A newborn cannot speak, read, or know what a namaste means. Fifteen years later, she debates in two languages. Socialisation made the difference.
p: Socialisation: the lifelong process by which a helpless infant gradually becomes a self-aware, knowledgeable person, skilled in the ways of the culture.
Cases of isolated or 'feral' children (such as the 'wild boy of Aveyron' found in France around 1800) show that without social contact, children do not develop normal language and social behaviour.
Primary socialisation: in early childhood, mainly in the family; the child learns language and basic behaviour. Secondary socialisation: later, through school, peers, work and wider society.
Re-socialisation: unlearning old norms and learning new ones when entering a new setting, e.g. joining the army, moving abroad.
Socialisation is not mere programming: individuals actively interpret, accept, question or resist what they learn.

ex.q: A young woman from Bihar joins the Indian Army. Trace her primary, secondary and re-socialisation.
st: Primary: family taught her language, values, manners in childhood.
Secondary: school, friends and college taught wider skills and norms.
Re-socialisation: army training replaces civilian habits with military discipline, rank-based conduct and new routines.
Throughout, she interprets and adapts rather than simply absorbing.
ex.a: Family gave primary socialisation; school and peers secondary; army training re-socialised her.

topics.rl: New recruits at the National Defence Academy, Khadakwasla, go through intense training that re-socialises them into military norms, a classic re-socialisation setting.

rv.summary: Socialisation is the lifelong process by which a helpless infant becomes a self-aware, skilled member of a culture; isolated children show social contact is essential. Primary socialisation happens in the family, secondary through school, peers and work, and re-socialisation in new settings.
focus: Meaning of socialisation and the feral-child evidence
remember: Primary: early childhood, mainly family; secondary: school, peers, work, wider society
Re-socialisation: unlearning old norms and learning new ones (army, moving abroad)
Individuals actively interpret, accept, question or resist what they learn
traps: Socialisation does not end at adulthood
Socialisation is not formal schooling alone

topics.t: Agencies of socialisation: family, peers and school
topics.h: Your family taught you to say 'please', your friends taught you the latest slang, and your school taught you to stand in line. Each is an agency of socialisation.
p: Family: the first agency; what children learn varies with family system (joint, nuclear), region and class.
Peer groups: relations among equals of similar age; they introduce age-grade norms and peer pressure, and allow negotiation that adult-child relations do not.
School: teaches the formal curriculum (subjects) and a hidden curriculum (e.g. obedience, punctuality, gender roles such as girls cleaning and boys lifting).
Exam skill: identify the socialising agents in your life and describe their role.

ex.q: List what each agency taught a Class 11 student, Aditi.
st: Family: language, food habits, respect for elders, religious practices.
Peers: music taste, slang, how to dress 'in style', handling peer pressure.
School: maths and science (formal), punctuality and queueing (hidden curriculum).
ex.a: Family gave basic values, peers gave age-group norms, school gave formal knowledge plus a hidden curriculum.

topics.rl: In many Indian schools, boys are asked to carry benches and girls to draw rangoli for events, a small but powerful hidden curriculum of gender roles.

rv.summary: The family is the first agency of socialisation, varying with family system, region and class. Peer groups of equals teach age-group norms and exert peer pressure. School teaches a formal curriculum and a hidden curriculum of obedience, punctuality and gender roles.
focus: Family, peers and school as agencies
remember: Family: first agency; varies by family system, region, class
Peer groups: relations among equals of similar age; age-grade norms, peer pressure
School: formal curriculum plus hidden curriculum (obedience, punctuality, gender roles)
traps: Schools do not teach only academic subjects
Peer relations are based on equality, not parent–child hierarchy

topics.t: Media, other agencies, gendered socialisation and freedom
topics.h: Ads tell girls to be 'fair' and 'delicate' and boys to be 'macho'. Yet many teens push back. Socialisation shapes us, but it also gives us the tools to question.
p: Mass media (print, radio, television, digital and social media) is a powerful agency; sociologists debate how far it shapes or merely reflects attitudes.
Other agencies include the workplace, neighbourhood, caste and class community, region and religion.

Gendered socialisation: boys and girls are raised with different expectations (toys, chores, freedom, emotions). Krishna Kumar's essay 'Growing up Male' discusses how boys are socialised into masculine roles.
Agencies of socialisation can conflict, e.g. school teaches gender equality while family norms differ, or media values clash with parents' values.
Socialisation is also the source of individuality: by learning language and ideas, people gain the ability to think independently and even challenge norms.

ex.q: Riya's school teaches gender equality, but at home she is told not to play cricket. Online she follows women cricketers. How do these agencies interact?
st: School: equality message.
Family: traditional gender norm.
Media: role models of women cricketers.
Agencies conflict; Riya interprets and chooses, showing socialisation can produce individuality.
ex.a: The agencies conflict, and through this Riya develops her own view: socialisation enables independent thinking.

topics.rl: The success of India's women cricketers, such as Mithali Raj and Harmanpreet Kaur, broadcast widely on television and social media, gives girls new role models that challenge older gendered socialisation.

rv.summary: Mass media is a powerful agency, though how far it shapes attitudes is debated; workplace, neighbourhood, caste, class, region and religion also socialise. Gendered socialisation raises boys and girls differently (Krishna Kumar's 'Growing up Male').
remember: Agencies: family, peers, school, mass media, workplace, neighbourhood, caste, class, region, religion
Gendered socialisation: different toys, chores, freedoms and emotions for boys and girls
Krishna Kumar, 'Growing up Male': boys socialised into masculine roles
traps: Sociologists do not agree that media completely determines attitudes
Socialisation does not produce only conformity

topics.ch: Understanding Society: Social Change and Social Order in Rural and Urban Society
topics.t: Social change: recent, rapid and significant
topics.h: Compress all of human existence into one 24-hour day. Agriculture appears at about 11:56 pm. Modern societies arrive only in the last 30 seconds before midnight. Yet look how much has changed in those 30 seconds!
p: Rapid, continuous social change is a recent phenomenon in human history. Anthony Giddens' clock analogy: if human existence were a 24-hour day, agriculture began around 11:56 pm, civilisations around 11:57 pm, and modern societies only at about 11:59:30 pm.
Social change must be studied together with social order, the forces that resist, slow down or regulate change.
Not every change is 'social change'. The term refers to significant change: change that is intensive (deeply alters the structure of society) and extensive (affects a large part of society).

Activity skill: list things that did not exist when your grandparents were young (smartphones, UPI, metro) and things that have disappeared from most homes (telegrams, kerosene lamps, long waits for a landline connection).

ex.q: Is a new hairstyle trend 'social change'? Is the spread of mobile phones? Explain.
st: Test 1, intensive: does it alter basic structures? A hairstyle: no. Mobile phones: yes, they reshaped communication, work and banking.
Test 2, extensive: does it affect large sections of society? A hairstyle: limited. Phones: hundreds of millions of people.
Only the second passes both tests.
ex.a: The hairstyle is a minor change; the spread of mobile phones is social change because it is both intensive and extensive.

topics.rl: India Post sent its last telegram in July 2013 after 163 years: one small sign of how communication changed within one lifetime.

rv.summary: Rapid, continuous social change is recent: in Giddens' 24-hour clock, modern societies appear only at about 11:59:30 pm. Social change means significant change — intensive and extensive — and must be studied together with social order.
focus: What counts as social change: intensive and extensive
Why change and order are studied together
remember: Clock analogy: agriculture ≈ 11:56 pm; civilisations ≈ 11:57 pm; modern societies ≈ 11:59:30 pm
Social change: intensive (deep) and extensive (wide) change
Social order: forces that resist, slow or regulate change
traps: Not every change is social change — a new hairstyle is trivial
Rapid change has not been a feature of all human history

topics.ch: Understanding Society: Social Change and Social Order in Rural and Urban Society
topics.h: Some changes creep in like a slow tide; others crash like a tsunami. Some change how society is built; others change how we think.
p: By nature or speed: evolutionary change is slow and gradual (from Darwin's theory of evolution); revolutionary change is rapid and sweeping, often political, e.g. the French or Russian Revolutions.
Social Darwinism applied 'survival of the fittest' to societies, claiming the 'fittest' groups deserved to dominate; it was used to justify inequality and is now rejected.
'Revolution' is also used for rapid change in other fields, e.g. the Industrial Revolution, the Green Revolution, the communications revolution.

By impact: structural change transforms the structure of society, e.g. the shift from gold and silver coins to paper money (and today digital money); change in ideas and values, e.g. new ideas about childhood that made child labour unacceptable.
Social change is hard to define precisely because almost everything changes; sociologists focus on significant change.

ex.q: Classify: (a) the shift from metal coins to paper money; (b) the growing belief that children should study, not work; (c) the French Revolution.
st: (a) changes how exchange is organised: structural change.
(b) changes values about childhood: change in ideas and values.
(c) rapid overthrow of monarchy: revolutionary change.
ex.a: (a) structural, (b) change in ideas and values, (c) revolutionary.

topics.rl: The Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009 and laws against child labour reflect a change in ideas and values about childhood.

rv.summary: Evolutionary change is slow and gradual; revolutionary change is rapid and sweeping, often political. Social Darwinism used 'survival of the fittest' to justify inequality and is rejected.
focus: Social Darwinism and why it is rejected
Structural change vs change in ideas and values
remember: Evolutionary: slow, gradual (from Darwin); revolutionary: rapid, sweeping (French, Russian Revolutions)
'Revolution' also used for Industrial, Green and communications revolutions
Structural change: coins → paper money; ideas and values: new view of childhood
traps: Social Darwinism is not accepted today
A change in values is not the same as structural change

topics.ch: Understanding Society: Social Change and Social Order in Rural and Urban Society
topics.t: Causes of change: environment, technology and economy
topics.h: Before the 1930s, the Gulf was known for pearl diving and trade. Then oil was found. Within decades, its societies were transformed.
p: Environmental causes: geography and climate shape ways of life, e.g. desert, cold mountain and river-valley societies differ greatly. Natural disasters like the 2004 tsunami can transform communities overnight.

Discovery of resources changes societies: the discovery of oil in West Asia transformed countries like Saudi Arabia, Kuwait and the UAE from relatively simple economies into wealthy, urbanised states.
Technological causes: steam power, railways and textile mills changed work and travel; technology can change society in unexpected ways.
Economic causes: plantation agriculture and the cotton trade moved labour across continents; today, world trade rules set through the World Trade Organization (WTO) affect farmers and industries.
Technology and economy are closely linked: new technology often changes economic organisation, and vice versa.

ex.q: Show how railways caused social change in colonial India.
st: Technology: steam railways connected distant regions.
Economy: raw materials moved to ports; British goods reached interiors.
Society: people of different castes travelled in the same carriages; migration for work grew.
So one technology triggered economic and social change.
ex.a: Railways changed trade, migration and even everyday social interaction across castes and regions.

topics.rl: Indian Railways, begun with the Bombay-Thane line in 1853, today carries crores of passengers daily and has reshaped migration, trade and pilgrimage.

rv.summary: Environment shapes ways of life, and disasters like the 2004 tsunami or resource discoveries like West Asian oil can transform societies. Technology such as steam power and railways changes society in unplanned ways, and economic forces from plantations to WTO trade rules reshape livelihoods.
focus: Economic causes and links with technology
remember: Environment: geography, climate, disasters (2004 tsunami); oil in West Asia transformed societies
Technology: steam power, railways, textile mills
Economy: plantation labour movements; WTO trade rules affect farmers and industries
traps: Technology does not have only its intended effects
A tsunami is environmental, not political or technological

topics.ch: Understanding Society: Social Change and Social Order in Rural and Urban Society
topics.t: Causes of change: political and cultural
topics.h: In India's first general election of 1951–52, a landless labourer and a former maharaja each had exactly one vote. One political decision changed the meaning of being Indian.
p: Political causes: wars, conquests, independence movements, the end of monarchies, and the coming of universal adult franchise (one person, one vote) transform societies.
Universal adult franchise gave every adult equal political rights regardless of caste, class or gender, changing power relations.
Cultural causes: religion and ideas can drive change, e.g. Weber's argument about the Protestant ethic and capitalism; the Bhakti movement challenging caste and ritual.
Changing ideas about women's status (education, work, property rights) have transformed families and workplaces.
Sport can be part of cultural change: cricket, once an elite colonial game, became a mass passion across India.
Exam skill: explain the role of environment, technology and economy, politics and culture in social change, with examples.

ex.q: Classify the main cause: (a) end of princely states after 1947; (b) Bhakti saints questioning caste; (c) women entering paid work in large numbers.
st: (a) change in political structure: political cause.
(b) religious ideas: cultural cause.
(c) changing ideas about women's status (with economic factors): cultural cause.
ex.a: (a) political; (b) cultural (religious ideas); (c) cultural, linked to the changing status of women.

topics.rl: Women's reservation in panchayats (73rd Amendment, 1992) brought lakhs of women into local politics, a political cause that also changed ideas about women's roles.

rv.summary: Political causes — wars, independence, the end of monarchies, universal adult franchise — transform societies; franchise gave every adult an equal vote. Cultural causes include religion (Weber's Protestant ethic, Bhakti), changing ideas about women's status, and even sport like cricket.
focus: Cultural causes: religion, women's status, sport
remember: Universal adult franchise: every adult citizen votes, regardless of caste, class or gender
Cultural causes: Protestant ethic, Bhakti movement, changing status of women
Cricket spread from a colonial elite game to a mass passion
traps: Political change does affect ideas and values
Bhakti is a cultural, not technological, cause

topics.ch: Understanding Society: Social Change and Social Order in Rural and Urban Society
topics.h: Imagine if traffic rules, exam rules and the meaning of money changed every morning. Chaos! Social order is what keeps life predictable.
p: Social order: the persisting patterns of behaviour and relationships in a society that resist and regulate change.
Dominant groups, who benefit from existing arrangements, tend to favour stability; subordinate groups more often seek change.
Order is maintained in two broad ways: spontaneous consent, through shared values and norms learned in socialisation; and coercion, through force, law and punishment.
In practice, most societies combine consent and coercion.
Thought experiment: if rules changed every day, no one could plan or cooperate, which shows why order matters.

ex.q: Why do most people stand in a queue at a railway ticket counter? Identify consent and coercion.
st: Consent: people have learned that queuing is fair and polite (shared value).
Coercion: a policeman or RPF guard may push queue-jumpers back; there may be rules.
Both together keep order.
ex.a: Mostly consent from shared norms of fairness, backed by some coercion from staff and rules.

topics.rl: Most Indians follow traffic signals because they accept them (consent), but cameras and e-challans add coercion; together they produce order on the roads.

rv.summary: Social order is the persisting patterns of behaviour that resist and regulate change. Dominant groups favour stability; subordinate groups seek change. Order rests on spontaneous consent through shared values and on coercion through force, law and punishment — usually both.
focus: Who favours stability and who seeks change
remember: Social order: persisting patterns of behaviour and relationships that resist and regulate change
Spontaneous consent: shared values and norms from socialisation
Coercion: force, law and punishment; most societies combine both
traps: Order is not only police action
Not all groups want stability equally

topics.ch: Understanding Society: Social Change and Social Order in Rural and Urban Society
topics.h: A judge in a black robe says 'Sentence: two years'. Nobody fights her; the convict walks away with the police. Why do people obey? Max Weber's answer: legitimacy.
p: Power: the ability to make others do what one wants, regardless of their wishes. Domination: power exercised in a stable, routine way.
Legitimacy: the acceptance of power as just and proper. Max Weber defined authority as legitimate power.
Law: an explicit, codified norm, written down and enforced by the state. Examples of authority: a judge, a police officer, a teacher, a tax official.
Informal authority exists too: religious or sect leaders and respected elders may hold authority without formal legal positions.

ex.q: Classify the source of authority: (a) a district collector, (b) a spiritual guru whose followers obey him, (c) a gang leader.
st: (a) Legal office, backed by law: formal authority.
(b) Accepted by followers but not by law: informal authority.
(c) Power without legitimacy (not accepted as just): not authority.
ex.a: (a) formal legal authority, (b) informal authority, (c) power without legitimacy.

topics.rl: When the Election Commission of India announces poll dates, parties, officials and voters comply. Its authority rests on constitutional legitimacy.

rv.summary: Power is the ability to make others obey regardless of their wishes; domination is power exercised in a stable, routine way. Legitimacy is acceptance of power as just, and Weber called legitimate power authority.
remember: Domination: power exercised in a stable, routine way
Legitimacy: acceptance of power as just and proper; authority = legitimate power (Weber)
Law: explicit, codified norm enforced by the state
traps: A thief exercises power, not authority
Law is not an unwritten custom

topics.ch: Understanding Society: Social Change and Social Order in Rural and Urban Society
topics.h: On 6 April 1930, Gandhi picked up a handful of salt at Dandi, deliberately breaking British law. Was it a crime? Legally, yes. Morally, millions said it was justice.
p: Contestation: dissent and disagreement with the established order. It ranges from debate, protest and counter-cultures (groups rejecting dominant values) to elections, where parties peacefully contest power.
Crime: an act that breaks a law. Whether something is a crime depends on the law, not on its morality.
Laws can be unjust and may be deliberately broken as a form of protest, e.g. Gandhi's Salt Satyagraha (1930) in civil disobedience against the salt law.
Violence is the extreme form of contestation. Max Weber noted that the modern state claims a monopoly over the legitimate use of violence (e.g. police, army).

ex.q: Classify: (a) a peaceful protest march with permission; (b) breaking the salt law at Dandi; (c) a riot; (d) a general election.
st: (a) dissent within the rules: contestation.
(b) deliberate breaking of an unjust law: crime in law, civil disobedience in purpose.
(c) extreme contestation using force: violence.
(d) peaceful, institutional contest for power: contestation through elections.
ex.a: (a) and (d) contestation, (b) a crime by law but morally framed as protest, (c) violence.

topics.rl: Gandhi's 1930 Salt March from Sabarmati Ashram to Dandi covered about 385 km and inspired mass civil disobedience across India.

rv.summary: Contestation is dissent against the established order, from debate, protest and counter-cultures to peaceful elections. Crime is breaking a law, defined by law not morality; unjust laws may be broken in protest, as in the 1930 Salt Satyagraha.
remember: Contestation: dissent and disagreement with the established order; includes counter-cultures and elections
Crime: an act that breaks a law; Salt Satyagraha (1930) broke the salt law in protest
Weber: the modern state claims a monopoly over the legitimate use of violence
traps: Not all crimes involve violence
Crime is defined by law, not by morality

topics.ch: Understanding Society: Social Change and Social Order in Rural and Urban Society
topics.h: When does a big village become a town? The Census of India has an answer, and it involves three numbers.
p: Villages emerged with settled agriculture, which produced a surplus and allowed people to stay in one place.
The rural-urban distinction rests on population density and the share of people in agricultural occupations: rural areas have lower density and more agricultural work.

Census of India: a town is either a statutory town (with a municipality, corporation, cantonment board or notified town area) or a census town meeting three tests: population at least 5,000; at least 75% of the male main working population in non-agricultural work; density at least 400 persons per sq km.

Urban agglomeration: a continuous urban spread made up of a town and its adjoining outgrowths (or two or more contiguous towns). A metropolitan city or area has a population of 10 lakh (1 million) or more.
India is urbanising: about 31% of Indians lived in urban areas in 2011, and the number of million-plus cities and agglomerations has grown (53 in 2011).

ex.q: A settlement has 6,000 people, 80% of male main workers in non-farm jobs, and density 350 persons per sq km. It has no municipality. Is it a census town?
st: Population ≥ 5,000? 6,000: yes.
≥ 75% male main workers non-agricultural? 80%: yes.
Density ≥ 400 per sq km? 350: no.
All three must be met, so it is not a census town.
ex.a: No: it fails the density test (350 is below 400).

topics.rl: Greater Mumbai, Delhi and Kolkata are among India's largest urban agglomerations; smaller census towns are growing fast around them as farmland turns into suburbs.

rv.summary: Villages arose with settled agriculture; rural areas have lower density and more farm work. A census town needs at least 5,000 people, 75% of male main workers in non-farm jobs and density of 400 per sq km. About 31% of Indians were urban in 2011.
focus: Origin of villages and the rural–urban distinction
Urban agglomeration and India's urban share
remember: Census town: population ≥ 5,000; ≥ 75% male main workers non-agricultural; density ≥ 400 per sq km
Urban agglomeration: town with outgrowths, or contiguous towns, forming one urban spread
Metropolitan: 10 lakh or more; about 31% urban in 2011
traps: All three census-town tests must be met, not just one or two
India's urban share in 2011 was about 31%, not 50%

topics.ch: Understanding Society: Social Change and Social Order in Rural and Urban Society
topics.t: Social order and change in rural areas
topics.h: In a village of 800 people, everyone knows whose son came home late last night. That closeness makes villages powerful keepers of social order.
p: Villages tend to have stronger social order: small size, face-to-face ties, little anonymity, and dependence on dominant groups for land, work and credit make change slower.

Traditional power structures: M.N. Srinivas used the term dominant caste for a caste that is numerically significant, owns much of the land and holds political and economic power locally; such castes control land, labour and local institutions.
Land reforms after Independence (abolition of zamindari, tenancy reforms, land ceilings) tried to weaken landlord power and give land to tillers; their success varied widely across states.
Where land reforms worked better, as in Kerala and West Bengal (Operation Barga), rural power relations shifted more.

ex.q: Why might a landless labourer in a village hesitate to protest against a large landowner?
st: Small village: everyone knows everyone; no anonymity.
Dependence: the landowner gives work, credit and perhaps housing.
Dominant caste: the landowner's group may control the panchayat and local institutions.
So social order is strong and resists change.
ex.a: Because face-to-face ties, dependence and dominant-caste control make protest risky.

topics.rl: West Bengal's Operation Barga (from 1978) recorded sharecroppers' rights, giving them security against eviction, a land reform that shifted rural power.

rv.summary: Villages have strong social order: small size, face-to-face ties, little anonymity and dependence on dominant groups. Srinivas's dominant caste is numerous, owns much land and holds local power. Land reforms tried to weaken landlords, with uneven success — strongest in Kerala and West Bengal.
focus: Why social order is strong in villages
Land reforms and their uneven results
remember: Dominant caste (M.N. Srinivas): numerically significant, owns much land, holds political and economic power
Land reforms: abolition of zamindari, tenancy reforms, land ceilings
Operation Barga in West Bengal; reforms more effective in Kerala and West Bengal
traps: Land reforms were not equally successful everywhere
A dominant caste is not a small landless group

topics.ch: Understanding Society: Social Change and Social Order in Rural and Urban Society
topics.t: Rural change: technology and state programmes
topics.h: In the 1960s, new wheat seeds, tubewells and tractors arrived in Punjab. Harvests soared, and so did changes in who worked, how they were paid, and who held power.
p: Technological change in agriculture (irrigation, tractors, high-yielding seeds, fertilisers, i.e. the Green Revolution) raised output in regions like Punjab, Haryana and western UP.
It changed labour relations: payment in kind gave way to cash wages, attached labour gave way to casual labour, and some machines reduced demand for labour.

The state runs development and employment programmes in rural areas. The Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act (MGNREGA), 2005 guarantees 100 days of wage employment a year to every rural household whose adult members volunteer for unskilled manual work.
Such schemes can raise wages and bargaining power, but face problems such as delayed payments, corruption and uneven implementation.
Activity skill: study a rural employment scheme's aims and problems.

ex.q: A family has four adults who want MGNREGA work. How many days of guaranteed employment does the household get in a year?
st: The guarantee is per household, not per person.
Each rural household gets up to 100 days a year.
So the four adults together share 100 days.
ex.a: 100 days for the household as a whole.

topics.rl: MGNREGA works include building ponds, check dams and rural roads; it was a key safety net when migrant workers returned to villages during the 2020 lockdown.

rv.summary: The Green Revolution's seeds, irrigation, tractors and fertilisers raised output in Punjab, Haryana and western UP and changed labour relations: cash wages and casual labour replaced payment in kind and attached labour. MGNREGA (2005) guarantees 100 days of work a year per rural household.
remember: Green Revolution: high-yielding seeds, irrigation, fertilisers, tractors
Labour: payment in kind → cash wages; attached → casual labour
MGNREGA 2005: 100 days of wage work per rural household per year
traps: The 100-day guarantee is per household, not per person
Farm technology did not have only economic effects

topics.ch: Understanding Society: Social Change and Social Order in Rural and Urban Society
topics.t: Urban life: anonymity, space, slums and ghettos
topics.h: In a Mumbai local train, you can stand pressed against 200 strangers and know none of their names. City life gives freedom, and loneliness, in equal measure.
p: Urbanism as a way of life (associated with Louis Wirth): large size, density and diversity create anonymity, individualism and impersonal relations, but also freedom from traditional controls.
Space is central to city life: who lives where reflects and reinforces divisions of class, caste, religion and ethnicity.
Slums: densely populated areas with poor housing and inadequate services (water, sanitation, electricity), housing many of the urban poor and migrants who often provide essential labour.
Ghettoisation: concentration of members of a particular community in an area, often because of discrimination or for a sense of security, especially after conflict.

ex.q: Explain why a migrant worker might feel both freer and more insecure in a city than in his village.
st: Freer: anonymity weakens caste and family controls; he can choose work and friends.
Insecure: impersonal relations, no village support network, slum housing with poor services.
This double effect is typical of urbanism as a way of life.
ex.a: Anonymity brings freedom from traditional controls, but impersonal life and slum conditions bring insecurity.

topics.rl: Dharavi in Mumbai, one of Asia's largest informal settlements, is also a hub of small industries such as leather, pottery and recycling: slums are places of both hardship and enterprise.

rv.summary: Louis Wirth's 'urbanism as a way of life' links large, dense, diverse cities to anonymity, individualism and impersonal ties, but also freedom from tradition.
focus: Urbanism as a way of life (Wirth)
Space and social divisions in cities
remember: Urbanism (Louis Wirth): anonymity, individualism, impersonal relations; freedom from traditional controls
Slums: dense areas with poor housing and inadequate water, sanitation, electricity
Ghettoisation: concentration of a community in one area, often for security after conflict
traps: Ghettoisation is not gentrification
Slums do not have adequate housing and services

topics.ch: Understanding Society: Social Change and Social Order in Rural and Urban Society
topics.h: Behind a boom barrier: a pool, a gym, 24-hour security. Outside: a busy road and a slum. A gated community is a city's inequality made visible.
p: Gated communities: enclosed, affluent residential enclaves with walls, guards and private services (water, power backup, security, parks), separating residents from the surrounding city.
Transport and commuting shape city life: long daily commutes, crowded local trains and buses, and new metro systems in many Indian cities. The poor often live far from work or near it in slums.
Gentrification: the upgrading of older, poorer neighbourhoods into middle- or upper-class areas, often displacing earlier residents who can no longer afford to live there.
Activity skill: ask who gains and who loses when a neighbourhood is gentrified or when gated communities spread.
Exam skill: compare social order and change in rural and urban areas.

ex.q: An old mill-workers' area in a city is redeveloped into malls and luxury flats. Who gains and who loses?
st: Gain: builders, new affluent residents, city revenue, shoppers.
Lose: old residents and small traders who are priced out and displaced.
This process is gentrification.
ex.a: Builders and affluent newcomers gain; poorer original residents lose through displacement.

topics.rl: Mumbai's suburban rail carries millions of passengers daily, and metro networks in Delhi, Bengaluru and other cities are reshaping where people live and work.

rv.summary: Gated communities are walled, affluent enclaves with private services that deepen spatial segregation. Long commutes shape city life. Gentrification upgrades poorer areas and displaces earlier residents. Rural order rests on face-to-face control and dependence; urban life on anonymity.
focus: Gentrification: who gains, who loses; rural vs urban order
remember: Gated community: enclosed affluent enclave with walls, guards and private services
Gentrification: upgrading poorer neighbourhoods, displacing earlier residents
Rural order: face-to-face control and dependence; urban: anonymity
traps: Gated communities do not rely only on public services
Gentrification is not ghettoisation

topics.t: The age of revolutions: Enlightenment and French Revolution
topics.h: 'Liberty, Equality, Fraternity!' shouted the crowds in Paris in 1789. Their slogan, and the ideas behind it, helped give birth to a brand-new science: sociology.
p: Sociology was born in 19th-century Western Europe as a product of the 'age of revolutions': the Enlightenment, the French Revolution and the Industrial Revolution.
The Enlightenment (late 17th and 18th centuries) promoted reason, secular, scientific and humanistic thinking, and placed the individual human being at the centre of the universe as the knower.

The French Revolution (1789) proclaimed political sovereignty for individuals and nations, and the ideals of liberty, equality and fraternity; it ended feudal bonds and the dominance of the Church over the state.
It also separated the public sphere (the state, citizenship) from the private sphere (home, family, religion), creating ideas of the modern citizen.
Exam skill: explain why these revolutions together shaped sociology: they made society itself appear changeable and open to rational study.

ex.q: Why did the French Revolution make people think about 'society' in a new way?
st: Before 1789: society seemed fixed by God, kings and feudal custom.
The Revolution overthrew monarchy and feudal privileges within a few years.
If society could be remade by humans, it could also be studied by humans.
This encouraged a science of society: sociology.
ex.a: It showed society was human-made and changeable, so it could be studied rationally.

topics.rl: The Indian Constitution's Preamble promises Liberty, Equality and Fraternity, ideals whose modern political form owes much to the French Revolution.

rv.summary: Sociology was born in 19th-century Western Europe from the 'age of revolutions'. The Enlightenment promoted reason and put the individual at the centre; the French Revolution (1789) proclaimed liberty, equality and fraternity, ended feudal privileges and separated public and private spheres.
remember: Enlightenment: reason, secular, scientific and humanistic thinking; the individual as knower
French Revolution, 1789: liberty, equality, fraternity; end of feudal bonds and Church dominance
Separation of public sphere (state, citizenship) from private sphere (home, family, religion)
traps: The French Revolution reduced, not strengthened, the Church's control
Sociology did not come from the Mughal period or the Cold War

topics.t: The Industrial Revolution and the 'science of the new industrial society'
topics.h: Factory chimneys, overflowing slums, cholera outbreaks: 19th-century European cities were full of problems no one had seen before. Sociology was invented to understand them.
p: The Industrial Revolution (from the late 18th century, beginning in Britain) applied science and technology to production and created new ways of organising labour and markets.
Social effects: factories drew people from villages to cities; urban poverty, slums, overcrowding and disease grew; workers lived in harsh conditions.
The state took on new responsibilities for public health, sanitation, and later education and welfare, and needed knowledge about society to do so.
Sociology emerged as the 'science of the new industrial society', responding to the need for systematic knowledge about these changes.

ex.q: Why did governments in 19th-century Europe need sociology-like knowledge?
st: Cities faced slums, epidemics and poverty.
Governments began to take responsibility for health, sanitation and welfare.
To act, they needed facts: who lived where, how many were poor, what caused disease.
Social surveys and new social sciences supplied such knowledge.
ex.a: To manage new urban problems, the state needed systematic social knowledge, which sociology provided.

topics.rl: The Swachh Bharat Mission and Smart Cities Mission are modern Indian examples of the state taking on sanitation and urban planning, needing social data to work.

rv.summary: The Industrial Revolution, starting in Britain, applied science and technology to production and reorganised labour. Factories created slums, poverty and disease, and states needing social knowledge gave rise to sociology as the 'science of the new industrial society'.
focus: Its social effects on cities and workers
remember: Industrial Revolution: science and technology applied to production; began in Britain
Effects: urban growth, slums, overcrowding, disease, harsh working conditions
Sociology: 'science of the new industrial society'
traps: The Industrial Revolution was not only economic — it transformed social life
It is not the same as the French Revolution

topics.t: Karl Marx: life, aims and base-superstructure
topics.h: Marx was expelled at different times from France, Belgium and Prussia before settling in London. From the reading room of the British Museum, he wrote a critique of capitalism that still sparks debate.
p: Karl Marx (1818–1883) was born in Trier, Germany. He moved through Paris and Brussels and settled in London. With Friedrich Engels he wrote The Communist Manifesto (1848); his major work is Capital (first volume 1867).
Marx's aim was to end exploitation and oppression. He called his approach 'scientific socialism' because he believed a scientific analysis of capitalism would show how it could be replaced.
He was a strong critic of capitalism, though he also recognised it as more productive than earlier systems.
Economic structure (the base) is the foundation of society; it shapes the superstructure of ideas, law, politics, religion and culture.

ex.q: Use base and superstructure to explain why laws in a capitalist society protect private property strongly.
st: Base: capitalist economy built on private ownership of means of production.
Superstructure: laws, politics and ideas.
According to Marx, the base shapes the superstructure.
So laws protecting private property reflect the capitalist base.
ex.a: Laws (superstructure) protect private property because they are shaped by the capitalist economic base.

topics.rl: Debates in India about labour codes, land laws and corporate taxes are often analysed by Marxist scholars as examples of the economic base shaping legal superstructure.

rv.summary: Karl Marx (1818–1883), born in Trier, wrote The Communist Manifesto (1848) with Engels and Capital (1867). Aiming to end exploitation, he called his approach scientific socialism. For Marx the economic base shapes the superstructure of ideas, law, politics and religion.
remember: Karl Marx: 1818–1883; The Communist Manifesto (1848, with Engels); Capital (vol. 1, 1867)
Scientific socialism: scientific analysis showing how capitalism could be replaced
Base = economic structure; superstructure = ideas, law, politics, religion, culture
traps: Marx did not see capitalism as just or permanent
Law and politics belong to the superstructure, not the base

topics.t: Modes of production and the stages of history
topics.h: Hunter-gatherers sharing food, slaves in Rome, serfs on a medieval manor, workers in a Manchester mill: for Marx, these are chapters in one long story of how humans produce.
p: Means (forces) of production: land, labour, tools, machinery, technology, energy and raw materials used to produce.
Relations of production: the economic relationships between people in production, especially who owns the means of production (e.g. master-slave, lord-serf, capitalist-worker).
Mode of production: the combination of means and relations of production; it defines a type of society.
Marx's stages of history: primitive communism, slavery, feudalism and capitalism, with an expected transition to socialism.
Each stage after primitive communism had two main opposed classes: masters and slaves, lords and serfs, capitalists and workers.

ex.q: Identify means and relations of production on a medieval manor.
st: Means: land, ploughs, oxen, serfs' labour.
Relations: lords own the land; serfs work it and owe labour or produce to the lord.
Together they form the feudal mode of production.
ex.a: Means: land, tools, labour; relations: lord-serf obligations; together they make up the feudal mode.

topics.rl: In a modern Indian textile mill, machines and electricity are means of production; the employer-worker wage relationship is the relation of production: together, a capitalist mode.

rv.summary: Means of production are land, labour, tools and technology; relations of production are economic ties, especially ownership. Together they form the mode of production. Marx's stages: primitive communism, slavery, feudalism, capitalism, then socialism.
focus: Means, relations and mode of production
remember: Means of production: land, labour, tools, machinery, technology, raw materials
Relations of production: economic relationships, especially ownership
Stages: primitive communism → slavery → feudalism → capitalism → (socialism)
traps: Marx did not think capitalism was the final stage
Lords and serfs belong to feudalism, not slavery

topics.h: A garment worker stitches 300 collars a day for a brand she will never afford, in a process she does not control, with co-workers she barely knows. Marx had a word for this: alienation.
p: For Marx, classes are groups of people who share the same position in the production process (e.g. owners or non-owners), and therefore share interests.

Under capitalism there are two main classes: the bourgeoisie (capitalists), who own the means of production, and the working class (proletariat), who own only their capacity to work and must sell their labour for wages.
The interests of these classes are opposed: capitalists seek profit, partly by keeping wages low; workers seek higher wages and better conditions.
Alienation: under capitalist production, workers are alienated (estranged) from the products they make, from the process of work, from fellow workers and from their own human potential.

ex.q: Show the forms of alienation in a garment worker's day.
st: From the product: she does not own or decide what happens to the clothes.
From the process: speed and tasks are set by managers and machines.
From fellow workers: they compete and are treated as interchangeable.
From her human potential: creative abilities are unused in repetitive tasks.
ex.a: She is alienated from the product, the process, co-workers and her own creative potential.

topics.rl: Gig workers on delivery apps in Indian cities often do not know their managers, are tracked by algorithms and are paid per task, a modern setting for debates on alienation.

rv.summary: For Marx, a class is people sharing a position in production. Under capitalism the bourgeoisie own the means of production and the proletariat own only their labour power, so their interests clash. Alienation estranges workers from their products, work, fellow workers and their own potential.
remember: Class: position in the production process (owners vs non-owners)
Bourgeoisie own the means of production; proletariat own only their capacity to work
Alienation: from product, process, fellow workers and own human potential
traps: Alienation does not mean being a foreigner
Workers do not own the means of production

topics.h: 'The history of all hitherto existing society is the history of class struggles.' This opening line of The Communist Manifesto sums up Marx's view of what drives history.
p: Shared economic position does not automatically make a group act together. Class consciousness, an awareness of shared interests and of opposition to another class, develops through political mobilisation and organisation.
Class struggle is the driving force of history: conflicts between classes push societies from one mode of production to another.
Revolution, in Marx's view, is the overthrow of a ruling class by an oppressed class, bringing a new mode of production.
Exam skill: explain Marx's ideas of class struggle and the role of economic structure (base) in shaping society.

ex.q: Why might factory workers who all earn low wages not protest together, and what could change this?
st: They share an objective class position (low-wage workers).
But they may be divided by region, language, caste or fear.
Unions and political mobilisation can create awareness of shared interests.
This awareness is class consciousness, which makes collective action possible.
ex.a: Shared position alone is not enough; political mobilisation builds the class consciousness needed for collective action.

topics.rl: Trade unions in India, such as those formed in Bombay's textile mills in the 1920s, organised workers across caste and region, an example of mobilisation building class consciousness.

rv.summary: Shared economic position does not automatically lead to joint action; class consciousness — awareness of shared interests — grows through political mobilisation. For Marx, class struggle drives history, and revolution is the overthrow of a ruling class by an oppressed class.
focus: Class consciousness and how it develops
Class struggle as the motor of history
remember: Class consciousness: awareness of shared interests and opposition, built through mobilisation
Class struggle drives history (The Communist Manifesto)
Revolution: overthrow of a ruling class by an oppressed class
traps: Class consciousness does not arise automatically from wages
For Marx, ideas are not the main cause of historical change

topics.h: Suicide feels like the most personal act there is. Durkheim showed that suicide rates rise and fall with social bonds, proving that even private acts have social patterns.
p: Emile Durkheim (1858–1917), born in Épinal, France, is regarded as a founder of sociology as a formal academic discipline. He founded the journal L'Année Sociologique.
Major works: The Division of Labour in Society (1893), The Rules of Sociological Method (1895), Suicide (1897) and The Elementary Forms of Religious Life (1912).
He argued sociology must have its own distinct subject matter: social facts.

Social facts are ways of acting, thinking and feeling that are external to the individual and exercise constraint over them, e.g. laws, language, moral codes, suicide rates. They should be studied scientifically, 'as things'.

ex.q: Is the rule that you must speak a language others understand a 'social fact'? Test it.
st: External: the language existed before you and will outlast you.
Constraint: if you invent your own words, no one understands you; you must conform.
Collective: it belongs to the group, not to one person.
So language is a social fact.
ex.a: Yes: language is external to the individual and constrains behaviour, so it is a social fact.

topics.rl: The National Crime Records Bureau's annual data on suicides show patterns by occupation, age and region, the kind of social facts Durkheim studied.

rv.summary: Emile Durkheim (1858–1917) founded sociology as an academic discipline and the journal L'Année Sociologique; his works include The Rules of Sociological Method (1895) and Suicide (1897).
remember: Durkheim: 1858–1917; L'Année Sociologique
Works: Division of Labour (1893), Rules of Sociological Method (1895), Suicide (1897), Elementary Forms (1912)
Social facts: external, constraining ways of acting, thinking and feeling — laws, language, suicide rates
traps: Social facts are not personal opinions
Suicide is not purely individual — its rates are social facts

topics.t: Society as a moral system: mechanical and organic solidarity
topics.h: In a small tribe, stealing a neighbour's goat might bring harsh public punishment. In a city, a business dispute ends with a court ordering compensation. Durkheim read society's glue from its laws.
p: Durkheim saw society as a moral system, held together by social solidarity. Solidarity cannot be observed directly, so he used observable indicators such as law.

Mechanical solidarity: found in small, simple societies; based on likeness (similar beliefs, work and lifestyles) and a strong collective conscience. Its law is repressive: punishment of offenders to express collective outrage.

Organic solidarity: found in large, modern societies; based on difference and interdependence created by the division of labour. Its law is restitutive: aims to restore things to how they were (compensation, repair).
Exam skill: compare mechanical and organic solidarity and explain how law indicates the type of solidarity.

ex.q: Classify: (a) a village where everyone farms, shares beliefs, and theft is punished by public humiliation; (b) a city where a doctor, a lawyer and a coder depend on one another and contract disputes end in compensation.
st: (a) likeness, strong collective conscience, punishing law: mechanical solidarity, repressive law.
(b) difference, interdependence through specialisation, compensation: organic solidarity, restitutive law.
ex.a: (a) mechanical solidarity with repressive law; (b) organic solidarity with restitutive law.

topics.rl: India's consumer courts order refunds or compensation for defective products, a clear example of restitutive law in a society bound by organic solidarity.

rv.summary: Durkheim read social solidarity through law. Mechanical solidarity in small societies rests on likeness and a strong collective conscience, with repressive law; organic solidarity in modern societies rests on difference and interdependence, with restitutive law.
remember: Mechanical: likeness, strong collective conscience; repressive law (punishment)
Organic: difference and interdependence from division of labour; restitutive law (compensation)
Solidarity is not directly visible, so law is used as its indicator
traps: Organic solidarity is not based on likeness
Restitutive law repairs harm; it does not punish to show outrage

topics.t: Division of labour and the rise of modern society
topics.h: A village a century ago had a few dozen occupations. Today, LinkedIn lists thousands. Durkheim argued this explosion of specialisation is what makes a society modern.
p: In The Division of Labour in Society, Durkheim used the division of labour to explain the shift from simple to modern societies.
As population and its density grow, people interact more and compete for resources; specialisation (division of labour) increases as a solution.
With more specialisation, people become different from one another, so the collective conscience weakens and becomes more general.
Modern society allows greater individual autonomy: individuals choose occupations, beliefs and voluntary associations (clubs, unions, NGOs) rather than having them fixed by the group.

ex.q: Trace Durkheim's chain from a growing population to individual freedom.
st: Population and density increase.
More interaction and competition.
Greater division of labour (specialisation).
People become more different; collective conscience weakens.
Individual autonomy and voluntary associations grow.
ex.a: Growing density leads to specialisation, which weakens the collective conscience and increases individual autonomy.

topics.rl: Bengaluru's mix of coders, delivery riders, start-up founders and classical musicians, each joining clubs and associations of choice, illustrates Durkheim's modern society of autonomy and interdependence.

rv.summary: In The Division of Labour in Society (1893), Durkheim explained the move to modern society: rising population density brings more interaction and competition, so specialisation grows.
focus: Durkheim's chain from density to specialisation
remember: Division of labour explains the shift from simple to modern society
Rising density → more competition → more specialisation → weaker collective conscience
Voluntary associations: groups people join by choice (clubs, unions, NGOs)
traps: Specialisation makes people more different, not more alike
The collective conscience weakens in modern society; it does not strengthen

topics.h: A raised hand could be a vote, a question, a greeting or a call for a taxi. You only know which if you understand what it means to the person raising it. That is Weber's starting point.
p: Max Weber (1864–1920), German sociologist, is best known for The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism (1904–05) and his studies of religion, authority and bureaucracy.
Interpretive sociology: sociology should understand social action, i.e. action guided by the subjective meanings actors attach to it.
Because humans act on meanings, the social sciences need methods different from those of the natural sciences.
Empathetic understanding (Verstehen): the sociologist puts himself or herself in the actor's place to grasp the meanings and motives, while recording them faithfully.
Value neutrality: sociologists should describe others' values and meanings objectively, without judging them by their own values.

ex.q: A researcher studies why young people in a town join a pilgrimage. How would Weber want her to proceed?
st: Focus on social action: what does joining mean to the pilgrims?
Use empathetic understanding: interview and observe, trying to see from their viewpoint.
Practise value neutrality: record meanings without judging whether the beliefs are right.
Compare patterns using concepts such as ideal types.
ex.a: Seek the pilgrims' own meanings through empathetic understanding, while staying value-neutral.

topics.rl: Ethnographers studying the Pandharpur Wari, the annual pilgrimage to Vitthal's temple in Maharashtra, try to understand what it means to the warkaris themselves: Weberian method in practice.

rv.summary: Max Weber (1864–1920), author of The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism, founded interpretive sociology: understanding social action through actors' subjective meanings. This needs methods unlike the natural sciences — empathetic understanding (Verstehen) and value neutrality.
remember: Max Weber: 1864–1920; The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism (1904–05)
Social action: action guided by subjective meanings
