Verstehen: putting oneself in the actor's place; value neutrality: describe values without judging
traps: Empathetic understanding is not sympathy or agreement
Weber did not want sociology to copy the natural sciences exactly

topics.t: Ideal type and types of authority
topics.h: A king obeyed because 'it has always been so', a leader obeyed because she seems extraordinary, an officer obeyed because rules say so. Weber built three neat ideal types out of messy reality.
p: Ideal type: a logically consistent model that exaggerates and highlights the key features of a social phenomenon. It is an analytical tool for comparison, not a description of any real case and not a moral 'ideal'.
Weber used ideal types to classify authority (legitimate power) into three types.
Traditional authority: based on custom and long-established practice, e.g. hereditary chiefs or kings.
Charismatic authority: based on the extraordinary personal qualities attributed to a leader by followers, e.g. prophets, revolutionary leaders.
Rational-legal authority: based on impersonal rules and legal procedures; obedience is owed to the office, not the person, e.g. bureaucrats, elected officials.

ex.q: Classify: (a) a hereditary raja obeyed by custom; (b) a magnetic leader whose followers believe he can transform the nation; (c) a district magistrate obeyed because of law.
st: (a) Custom and inheritance: traditional authority.
(b) Extraordinary personal qualities: charismatic authority.
(c) Legal rules and office: rational-legal authority.
ex.a: (a) traditional, (b) charismatic, (c) rational-legal.

topics.rl: An IAS officer transferred from one district to another loses authority in the first and gains it in the second: obedience follows the office, the mark of rational-legal authority.

rv.summary: An ideal type is a logical model that exaggerates key features for comparison, not a moral ideal. Weber classed authority into traditional (custom, hereditary rulers), charismatic (extraordinary personal qualities) and rational-legal (impersonal rules; obedience to the office).
focus: What an ideal type is and is not
remember: Ideal type: logically consistent model highlighting key features; an analytical tool
Traditional: custom; charismatic: extraordinary qualities; rational-legal: impersonal rules and office
In rational-legal authority, power belongs to the office, not the person
traps: 'Ideal' does not mean 'best'
Ideal types do not describe any real leader perfectly

topics.h: File number 47/B moves from the clerk to the section officer to the under-secretary, each stamping it within their powers. Annoying? Maybe. But Weber said this is how modern rational authority works.
p: Bureaucracy is the typical organisation of rational-legal authority; it separates the public office from the private life of the official.
Functioning of officials: each office has a fixed area of jurisdiction, with duties and powers defined by rules.
Hierarchical ordering of positions: a clear chain of command, with lower offices supervised by higher ones.
Reliance on written documents (files): decisions and records are kept in writing.
Office management by trained, specialised staff; and disciplined conduct in office: the official works full-time, follows rules, and does not use the office for private benefit.

ex.q: Check whether your school office is a bureaucracy against Weber's features.
st: Fixed jurisdiction: accounts clerk handles fees, admissions clerk handles forms.
Hierarchy: clerks report to the office superintendent, who reports to the principal.
Written documents: registers, files, receipts.
Trained staff and rules: staff are recruited for skills and follow written procedures.
Separation of office and private life: fees go into school accounts, not the clerk's pocket.
ex.a: Yes: it shows jurisdiction, hierarchy, written files, trained staff and separation of office from private life.

topics.rl: Indian Railways, with its zones, divisions, written circulars and recruitment by exam, is one of the world's largest bureaucracies.

rv.summary: Bureaucracy is the typical organisation of rational-legal authority and separates the office from the official's private life. Its features: fixed jurisdiction of each office, hierarchy, written documents (files), trained specialised staff, and disciplined full-time conduct by rules.
focus: Applying the features to a real office
remember: Fixed area of jurisdiction: duties and powers defined by rules
Hierarchical ordering; reliance on written documents (files)
Trained, specialised staff; office separated from private life
traps: Officials may not use their office for private benefit
Bureaucracy is not linked to charismatic authority

topics.h: Sociology arrived in India while the British still ruled it. Indian scholars soon asked a sharp question: can a discipline born in Europe explain a society like ours?
p: Sociology in India began under colonial rule. It was first taught at the University of Bombay from 1919; in the 1920s the universities of Calcutta and Lucknow also started teaching it.

Early Indian sociologists faced questions such as: What is colonial modernity? Is social anthropology (Western study of 'other' cultures) relevant when Indians study their own society? What role can sociology play in building a new nation?

Each founder 'Indianised' the discipline in a distinct way: Ghurye through caste and tribe, D.P. Mukerji through tradition, A.R. Desai through Marxism and the state, M.N. Srinivas through village fieldwork.
We study the founders critically, not as unquestionable authorities, so that later generations can build on and revise their work.

ex.q: Why was 'social anthropology' an awkward fit for Indian scholars studying India?
st: Western anthropology studied distant 'primitive' others.
Indian scholars were studying their own society, often their own region or community.
They had to rethink the subject's assumptions and adapt it to Indian realities.
This is part of 'Indianising' the discipline.
ex.a: Because it was built to study distant 'others', while Indians were studying their own society; they had to adapt it.

topics.rl: The University of Mumbai's Department of Sociology, among the oldest in India, traces its roots to 1919, when sociology began to be taught at Bombay.

rv.summary: Sociology in India began under colonial rule — taught at Bombay from 1919, then Calcutta and Lucknow in the 1920s. Early scholars asked whether Western social anthropology fitted Indians studying India, and each founder 'Indianised' the discipline in a different way.
focus: Questions faced by early Indian sociologists
How each founder Indianised sociology; studying founders critically
remember: Bombay University from 1919; Calcutta and Lucknow in the 1920s
Ghurye — caste and tribe; D.P. Mukerji — tradition; A.R. Desai — Marxism and state; M.N. Srinivas — village fieldwork
Founders should be studied critically, so later scholars can build on them
traps: Sociology did not begin in India only after Independence
Indianising did not mean rejecting all Western ideas

topics.t: The pioneers: Ananthakrishna Iyer, Sarat Chandra Roy and the administrators
topics.h: A clerk in Cochin and a lawyer in Ranchi never planned to become famous anthropologists. Curiosity, and the people around them, changed their careers.
p: Many early Indian anthropologists entered the field almost by accident, without formal training.

L.K. Ananthakrishna Iyer (1861–1937) began as a clerk, then a school and college teacher in Cochin. He volunteered to help with an ethnographic survey of Cochin State, became a recognised scholar, and helped set up the first post-graduate anthropology department in India at the University of Calcutta.

Sarat Chandra Roy (1871–1942) was a lawyer in Ranchi who became an official interpreter in court. Wanting to understand the tribal people whose cases he handled, he studied the Oraon, Munda and Kharia, and founded the journal Man in India, the earliest journal of its kind in India.
British administrator-anthropologists, such as H.H. Risley, Edgar Thurston, J.H. Hutton and William Crooke, conducted surveys and censuses, partly to help colonial administration.
Exam skill: explain how Iyer and Roy came to practise social anthropology.

ex.q: Why did Sarat Chandra Roy start studying tribal societies?
st: He worked as a lawyer and court interpreter in Ranchi.
He had to interpret tribal customs and laws in legal cases.
To do this well, he studied tribal culture and society in depth.
His interest grew into lifelong ethnographic research.
ex.a: His court work required understanding tribal customs, which led him to systematic ethnography.

topics.rl: Ranchi today is the capital of Jharkhand, a state formed in 2000, home to the Munda, Oraon and other communities whom Roy studied a century earlier.

rv.summary: Many early Indian anthropologists entered the field by accident. L.K. Ananthakrishna Iyer, a clerk turned teacher in Cochin, joined an ethnographic survey and helped found India's first post-graduate anthropology department at Calcutta.
focus: How Iyer and Roy came to anthropology
remember: Ananthakrishna Iyer (1861–1937): clerk, teacher, Cochin ethnographic survey; first PG anthropology department, Calcutta
Sarat Chandra Roy (1871–1942): lawyer and court interpreter, Ranchi; Oraon, Munda, Kharia; founded Man in India
Administrator-anthropologists: H.H. Risley, Edgar Thurston, J.H. Hutton, William Crooke
traps: Iyer and Roy were not formally trained anthropologists at the start
Man in India was founded by Roy, not Ghurye

topics.t: G.S. Ghurye: founder of institutional sociology
topics.h: For 35 years one man headed India's first post-graduate sociology department and trained a whole generation of sociologists. His name: Govind Sadashiv Ghurye.
p: G.S. Ghurye (1893–1983) is regarded as the founder of institutionalised sociology in India. He headed the sociology department at Bombay University for 35 years (1924–1959).
He founded the Indian Sociological Society and its journal Sociological Bulletin.
He studied at Cambridge under W.H.R. Rivers and A.C. Haddon; his Ph.D. thesis was published as Caste and Race in India (1932).
Influences on his work: diffusionism (the idea that cultural traits spread from one culture to others), Orientalist scholarship on Hindu religion and texts, and nationalism.

ex.q: Why is Ghurye called the founder of 'institutionalised' sociology, rather than the first person to study Indian society?
st: Others (administrators, Iyer, Roy) had studied Indian society before him.
Ghurye built institutions: a long-running department, a professional society and a journal.
Institutions train students and sustain the discipline beyond one person.
So his key contribution was making sociology a lasting academic field.
ex.a: Because he built the department, society and journal that made sociology a lasting discipline in India.

topics.rl: The Indian Sociological Society, which Ghurye founded, still holds the All India Sociological Conference, bringing together sociologists from across the country.

rv.summary: G.S. Ghurye (1893–1983), founder of institutionalised sociology in India, headed Bombay's department for 35 years (1924–1959) and founded the Indian Sociological Society and Sociological Bulletin. Trained at Cambridge under Rivers and Haddon, he wrote Caste and Race in India (1932).
remember: Ghurye headed Bombay department 1924–1959 (35 years)
Founded Indian Sociological Society and Sociological Bulletin
Influences: diffusionism, Orientalist scholarship on Hinduism, nationalism
traps: Ghurye did not found Man in India — that was S.C. Roy
Weber's bureaucracy was not one of the listed influences on Ghurye

topics.h: Should India's tribal communities be protected from the outside world, or brought into the national mainstream? This question split scholars in the 1930s and 40s, and still matters today.
p: Protectionist view (many British administrator-anthropologists; Verrier Elwin was its best-known voice): tribes were distinct, vulnerable communities who needed protection from exploitation by traders, moneylenders and the wider Hindu society; hence a policy of keeping them relatively separate.
Nationalist view: the British were using protection to keep tribes apart and 'divide and rule'; tribes should be integrated into the Indian mainstream and share in development.
Ghurye argued tribes were 'backward Hindus' rather than distinct cultural groups, since they had long interacted with Hindu society and were further behind in the same process of assimilation.
The debate connects to later issues: tribal movements, the creation of states such as Jharkhand and Chhattisgarh (2000), and displacement by dams, mines and industries.
Exam skill: state the arguments on both sides of the tribal debate.

ex.q: Lay out both sides of the tribal debate in a table-like comparison.
st: Protectionists: tribes are distinct; contact brings exploitation and cultural loss; protect and keep apart.
Nationalists (incl. Ghurye): separation is a colonial tactic; tribes have long interacted with Hindu society; integrate them.
Ghurye's specific claim: tribes are 'backward Hindus'.
Today: debates on autonomy, development and displacement continue.
ex.a: Protectionists favoured isolation to prevent exploitation; nationalists, including Ghurye, favoured integration, with Ghurye calling tribes 'backward Hindus'.

topics.rl: The Fifth and Sixth Schedules of the Constitution and the Forest Rights Act, 2006 reflect ongoing efforts to balance protection of tribal rights with development.

rv.summary: In the tribe debate, protectionists (with Verrier Elwin the best-known voice) wanted tribes kept relatively separate to prevent exploitation. Nationalists saw this as divide and rule and wanted integration; Ghurye called tribes 'backward Hindus'.
remember: Protectionists: tribes are distinct and vulnerable; protect and keep apart (Verrier Elwin)
Nationalists: protection was divide and rule; integrate tribes into the mainstream
Ghurye: tribes are 'backward Hindus', long interacting with Hindu society
traps: Protectionists did not think outside contact would benefit tribes
Ghurye was a nationalist, not a protectionist, voice

topics.t: Risley's racial theory and Ghurye's critique
topics.h: Colonial officials once measured noses and skulls to rank castes by 'race'. Ghurye took their own data and showed the theory did not hold for most of India.
p: H.H. Risley, a colonial administrator, argued that caste originated in race. Using anthropometry (measurement of the human body, e.g. nose width and head shape), he claimed upper castes were of Aryan origin and lower castes of non-Aryan origin.
Ghurye did not reject the data entirely but showed Risley's thesis was only partially correct.
It broadly applied only to north India ('Hindustan proper'); in other regions, the anthropometric differences between castes were small, suggesting long mixing of groups.
Ghurye also pointed out that caste-wise averages could hide wide variation within each caste.
Today, race-based explanations of caste are rejected in sociology; caste is understood as a social institution.

ex.q: How did Ghurye use Risley's own type of evidence against him?
st: Risley: body measurements show upper castes are 'Aryan', lower 'non-Aryan'.
Ghurye examined anthropometric data region by region.
Clear differences appeared broadly only in north India.
Elsewhere castes differed little, so caste could not simply be a matter of race.
ex.a: He showed that the anthropometric pattern held broadly only for north India, so race could not explain caste across India.

topics.rl: Modern genetic studies of Indian populations also show long histories of mixing among groups, consistent with the view that caste is a social, not a racial, institution.

rv.summary: H.H. Risley used anthropometry to claim caste came from race — upper castes Aryan, lower non-Aryan. Ghurye showed the thesis was only partly correct: it held broadly only in north India, castes elsewhere differed little after long mixing, and averages hid variation.
remember: Risley: caste originated in race; anthropometry (nose width, head shape)
Ghurye: thesis applied broadly only to north India ('Hindustan proper')
Caste-wise averages can hide wide variation within each caste
traps: Ghurye did not reject anthropometric data completely
Risley's pattern did not hold in south India

topics.h: Ghurye didn't give a one-line definition of caste. He listed six features that, taken together, describe how the caste system worked.
p: 1. Segmental division: society is divided into closed, mutually exclusive segments (castes), membership fixed by birth.
2. Hierarchical division: castes are ranked from 'pure' to 'impure'. 3. Restrictions on social interaction, especially on sharing food, based on ideas of purity and pollution.
4. Differential rights and duties for different castes (in religion, dress, residence and other areas). 5. Restricted choice of occupation: occupations were hereditary.
6. Strict restrictions on marriage: caste endogamy (marrying within the caste), often with exogamy rules within it.

Glossary: anthropometry (body measurement), assimilation (absorption into a larger group), endogamy, exogamy, laissez-faire (minimal state interference in the economy), living tradition, welfare state.

ex.q: Match each situation to one of Ghurye's features: (a) a person can only marry within the caste; (b) a family must continue a hereditary trade; (c) food is not accepted from certain castes.
st: (a) marriage restricted to the caste: restriction on marriage (endogamy).
(b) hereditary trade: restricted choice of occupation.
(c) food rules based on purity: restriction on social interaction.
ex.a: (a) restrictions on marriage, (b) restricted occupational choice, (c) restrictions on social interaction (food).

topics.rl: The Constitution abolishes untouchability (Article 17) and guarantees freedom of occupation (Article 19(1)(g)), legally rejecting several features of caste that Ghurye described.

rv.summary: Ghurye described caste through six features: segmental division by birth, hierarchy from pure to impure, restrictions on social interaction such as food, differential rights and duties, restricted choice of occupation, and restrictions on marriage (caste endogamy).
remember: Six features: segmental division, hierarchy, restrictions on interaction, differential rights and duties, restricted occupation, marriage restrictions
Segmental division: closed, birth-based segments
Laissez-faire: minimal state interference in the economy
traps: Caste segments were not open to change at will
Ghurye listed six features, not five or eight

topics.h: D.P. Mukerji said the first duty of an Indian sociologist is to study the social traditions to which he or she belongs. You cannot understand India from a borrowed textbook alone.
p: D.P. Mukerji (1894–1961) taught at Lucknow University and, with Radhakamal Mukerjee and D.N. Majumdar, formed the Lucknow school of sociology. His works include Modern Indian Culture (1942), Problems of Indian Youth (1946) and Diversities (1958).
He argued that India's distinctive feature was its social system: India had, so to speak, 'too much' society, and too little of the individualism found in the West.
So Indian sociologists must be rooted in Indian social traditions and know them well, including the languages and customs of the people.
Living tradition: a tradition that maintains links with the past while adapting to the new, absorbing change without losing its identity.
Mukerji was deeply influenced by Marxism, but he believed it had to be adapted to Indian conditions.

ex.q: Is a family that celebrates Diwali with eco-friendly diyas, online greetings and the old Lakshmi puja a 'living tradition'? Explain.
st: Link with the past: the puja and festival continue.
Adapting to the new: eco-friendly materials and digital greetings.
It changes without losing its identity.
This is exactly Mukerji's living tradition.
ex.a: Yes: it keeps links with the past while adapting to new conditions.

topics.rl: Classical music gharanas that now teach online, keeping old compositions while reaching new students, are living traditions in Mukerji's sense.

rv.summary: D.P. Mukerji (1894–1961) of the Lucknow school, with Radhakamal Mukerjee and D.N. Majumdar, held that India's distinctive feature is its social system, so sociologists must be rooted in Indian traditions. A living tradition keeps links with the past while adapting to the new.
focus: Mukerji's view of India's social system
remember: D.P. Mukerji: Lucknow University; works: Modern Indian Culture (1942), Problems of Indian Youth (1946), Diversities (1958)
India has 'too much' society; sociologists must know Indian traditions
Living tradition: keeps links with the past while adapting to the new
traps: A living tradition is not static
Mukerji was at Lucknow, not Bombay or Baroda

topics.t: D.P. Mukerji on change: shruti, smriti and anubhava
topics.h: Kabir never wrote a scripture, yet his couplets changed how millions thought about caste and god. D.P. Mukerji would call that the power of anubhava, experience.
p: Mukerji argued that change in India comes through group and caste experience rather than class conflict, because class consciousness was weak and caste and group identities were strong.
Indian tradition recognises three principles: shruti (what is heard, revealed scripture), smriti (what is remembered, texts and codes based on tradition) and anubhava (personal experience).
Of these, anubhava is the revolutionary principle: experience can challenge established ideas.
In practice, it is the generalised anubhava, the collective experience of groups, that drives change; e.g. the Bhakti saints and Sufi saints whose experiences challenged orthodoxy and hierarchy.
Activity skill: trace changes in games, festivals or dress across generations in your family to see how traditions adapt.

ex.q: Classify the source of authority: (a) the Vedas, (b) Dharmashastra codes, (c) a Bhakti saint's personal devotional experience.
st: (a) revealed, 'heard' scripture: shruti.
(b) remembered tradition and codes: smriti.
(c) personal experience: anubhava, the revolutionary principle.
ex.a: (a) shruti, (b) smriti, (c) anubhava.

topics.rl: Sufi shrines like Ajmer Sharif and the Bhakti traditions of saints like Mirabai and Tukaram drew people across caste and community lines, examples of collective experience reshaping tradition.

rv.summary: Mukerji held that change in India comes through group and caste experience, not class conflict, since class consciousness was weak. Of shruti (revealed scripture), smriti (remembered tradition) and anubhava (experience), anubhava is revolutionary, especially as collective group experience.
focus: Why Mukerji did not see class conflict as India's main source of change
Generalised anubhava and the Bhakti saints
remember: Shruti: what is heard (revealed scripture); smriti: what is remembered (texts, codes)
Anubhava: experience — the revolutionary principle
Generalised anubhava: collective experience of groups drives change
traps: Anubhava is not revealed scripture — that is shruti
Change in India was not mainly through class conflict in Mukerji's view

topics.t: A.R. Desai and the welfare state
topics.h: Many governments call themselves welfare states. A.R. Desai, a Marxist sociologist, set out tests to check whether they really were.
p: A.R. Desai (1915–1994) was a Marxist sociologist, known for his book Social Background of Indian Nationalism (1948), which analysed Indian nationalism using Marxist ideas.

He described the welfare state as having three features: (1) a positive state that actively uses its powers to implement social policies (not laissez-faire); (2) a democratic state, with democracy considered essential; (3) a mixed economy, where private and public enterprises co-exist.

Desai's tests of a welfare state: freedom from poverty, social discrimination and insecurity for all citizens; removal of inequalities of income through redistribution; transforming the economy so that community needs come before profit; stable development free from economic booms and busts; and employment for all.

ex.q: Apply two of Desai's tests to a country that has free schools but high unemployment and growing income inequality.
st: Test: employment for all. High unemployment: fails.
Test: reducing income inequality. Growing inequality: fails.
Free schools help reduce insecurity, but overall the state falls short.
ex.a: It fails at least two of Desai's tests (employment for all, reducing income inequality).

topics.rl: India's directive principles, schemes like the Public Distribution System and MGNREGA, and public sector undertakings are often discussed as welfare-state features against Desai's tests.

rv.summary: A.R. Desai (1915–1994), a Marxist sociologist, wrote Social Background of Indian Nationalism (1948). He described the welfare state as positive, democratic and a mixed economy, and tested it against goals like ending poverty, reducing inequality and jobs for all.
focus: Three features of the welfare state
Desai's tests of a welfare state
remember: Desai: Marxist; Social Background of Indian Nationalism (1948)
Features: positive (interventionist) state, democratic state, mixed economy
Tests: freedom from poverty, discrimination and insecurity; less income inequality; community needs before profit; stable development; employment for all
traps: Desai's welfare state is not laissez-faire
Maximising private profit is not one of his tests

topics.t: Desai's critique of the welfare state
topics.h: After applying his tests to Britain, the USA and other advanced countries, Desai reached a bold verdict: the welfare state is largely a myth.
p: Desai found that even advanced capitalist countries such as Britain and the USA failed many of his tests: poverty, inequality and unemployment persisted, and economic booms and busts continued.
He concluded that the welfare state is largely a myth: it does not deliver on its promises under capitalism.
He also criticised communist states, which in his view did not adequately protect democracy and freedoms, even if they provided some economic security.
Activity skill: list state services in your area (schools, hospitals, rations, transport) and ask how different classes use and view them.
Exam skill: explain the welfare state and Desai's criticism of it.

ex.q: A rich family uses private hospitals; a poor family depends on a government hospital with long queues. What would Desai's approach highlight?
st: Different classes relate differently to state services.
If public services are weak, the poor gain little security.
Unequal access suggests the state is not removing class inequality.
This supports Desai's view that the welfare state falls short.
ex.a: It would highlight class differences in access, supporting Desai's critique that welfare promises are not fully met.

topics.rl: Comparing how a family uses Ayushman Bharat cards, ration shops and government schools with how another uses private alternatives is a ready-made Desai-style class analysis.

rv.summary: Applying his tests to Britain, the USA and other advanced capitalist countries, Desai found poverty, inequality, unemployment and booms and busts persisting, and concluded the welfare state is largely a myth. He also faulted communist states for not protecting democracy and freedoms.
focus: Why the welfare state is 'largely a myth'
Criticism of communist states; class and state services
remember: Advanced capitalist countries failed many of Desai's tests
Verdict: the welfare state is largely a myth under capitalism
Communist states criticised for not protecting democracy and freedoms
traps: Desai did not think poverty was solved in Britain and the USA
His critique did not spare communist states

topics.h: In 1970, a fire destroyed M.N. Srinivas's field notes on the village of Rampura. He rewrote the village from memory, and The Remembered Village became a classic.
p: M.N. Srinivas (1916–1999) studied under Ghurye at Bombay and then at Oxford under A.R. Radcliffe-Brown and E.E. Evans-Pritchard.

He built major institutions: the sociology department at M.S. University of Baroda, the Department of Sociology at the Delhi School of Economics, and the Institute for Social and Economic Change in Bangalore.
Village studies were a central field of Indian sociology in the 1950s and 1960s, with scholars such as Srinivas (Rampura, Mysore), S.C. Dube and D.N. Majumdar.
Concepts linked to Srinivas include the dominant caste and Sanskritisation (a lower caste adopting the customs and practices of higher castes to raise its status).
Village studies showed the value of ethnographic fieldwork and documented rapid change in rural India as a new nation developed.

ex.q: Why were village studies so important for Indian sociology in the 1950s and 60s?
st: Most Indians lived in villages, so villages were central to understanding India.
Fieldwork gave first-hand evidence instead of colonial stereotypes.
They recorded how land reform, development and democracy were changing rural life.
They trained a generation in ethnographic methods.
ex.a: They used fieldwork to give first-hand evidence about rural India and documented change in a new nation.

topics.rl: About two-thirds of Indians still lived in rural areas in the 2011 Census, so village-level research remains essential for understanding India.

rv.summary: M.N. Srinivas (1916–1999) studied under Ghurye and at Oxford under Radcliffe-Brown and Evans-Pritchard, built departments at Baroda and Delhi and ISEC Bangalore, and studied Rampura. He gave the concepts of dominant caste and Sanskritisation; village studies flourished in the 1950s–60s.
remember: Srinivas: Ghurye (Bombay) then Oxford (Radcliffe-Brown, Evans-Pritchard)
Institutions: M.S. University of Baroda, Delhi School of Economics, ISEC Bangalore
Sanskritisation: lower caste adopting higher-caste customs to raise status; fieldwork at Rampura
traps: Sanskritisation does not mean learning the Sanskrit language
Srinivas's training was not only Western

topics.t: The village debate: Srinivas versus Dumont
topics.h: Is the Indian village a real community, or just a place where different castes happen to live? Two great scholars, M.N. Srinivas and Louis Dumont, disagreed sharply.
p: Louis Dumont, a French social anthropologist, argued that the village was merely a collection of people living in one place; caste was the real social unit and institution.
Srinivas argued that the village was a real and relevant social unit, with its own unity and identity.
Srinivas also showed that the village had changed historically and was never the unchanging, self-sufficient 'little republic' described by some British administrators.
Village studies thus corrected colonial stereotypes and showed rural India as dynamic.
Clues that a place is a village: most people work in agriculture, the population is small and less dense, and relations are face-to-face.
Activity skills: identify the clues that tell you a place is a village; discuss whether urban Indians still care about villages.

ex.q: A villager says, 'I am a Brahmin, but first I am from Rampura.' Whose view does this support?
st: Dumont: caste is the real unit, village is a mere collection.
Srinivas: the village is a real unit with its own identity.
The villager identifies strongly with the village.
This supports Srinivas's view.
ex.a: It supports Srinivas: the village is a meaningful unit of identity.

topics.rl: Many city dwellers still return to their native villages for festivals, weddings and elections, a living link that keeps the 'village versus city' debate alive.

rv.summary: Louis Dumont, a French anthropologist, saw the village as a mere collection of people, with caste the real unit. Srinivas saw the village as a real social unit and showed it had changed and was never a self-sufficient 'little republic' as colonial administrators claimed.
focus: Dumont's vs Srinivas's view of the village
Clues that a place is a village
remember: Dumont (French): village a mere collection; caste the real institution
Srinivas: village a real and relevant unit with identity; it changed historically
Village clues: mostly agricultural work, small less-dense population, face-to-face relations
traps: The 'little republic' image came from colonial administrators, not Srinivas
Villages were never fully self-sufficient or unchanging

qa.q: Which statement best captures the sociological view of a student's career choice?
qa.a: It is shaped by both individual effort and wider social forces
qa.e: Sociology recognises individual effort but shows how the job market, gender, class and family also shape choices.

qa.q: 'Arts is a good subject for girls; boys should do engineering.' Sociologically, this advice reflects:
qa.a: Gender expectations in society
qa.e: Linking subjects to gender is a social expectation, not a natural law.

qa.q: A sociologist asks, 'Who decides what counts as a good job?' This shows that sociology:
qa.a: Questions meanings that people take for granted
qa.e: Sociology examines everyday assumptions and asks where they come from.

qa.q: Finding out by observing and checking actual evidence is called:
qa.a: Empirical investigation
qa.e: Empirical means based on observation and evidence that others can check.

qa.q: Which of these is NOT one of the social factors that can affect a student's success?
qa.a: The colour of the student's school bag
qa.e: Class, gender and job markets are social forces; a bag's colour is irrelevant.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The advice students receive about subjects is often shaped by the job market.
Reason (R): Subjects linked to well-paid jobs are usually seen as more 'useful' by families.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true, and the perceived link between subjects and good jobs explains why the market shapes advice.

qa.q: Case: Ravi, from a family that cannot afford coaching, fails to clear an entrance exam that his richer classmate clears. A sociologist would most likely point to:
qa.a: Unequal access to resources linked to social class
qa.e: Sociology looks at structured differences such as class, which affect who can pay for coaching.

qa.q: 'Social constraint' refers to:
qa.a: The ways society limits and pressures individual choices
qa.e: Social constraint is pressure from social norms, institutions and expectations on what we do.

qa.q: Who gave the idea of the 'sociological imagination'?
qa.a: C. Wright Mills
qa.e: Mills used the term for linking personal biography to wider history and social structure.

qa.q: The sociological imagination helps us to grasp the relationship between:
qa.a: Biography and history
qa.e: Mills said it lets us see how individual lives connect with large-scale social change.

qa.q: In Mills' terms, mass unemployment caused by an economic slump is a:
qa.a: Public issue of social structure
qa.e: When many are affected and the cause lies in the economy, it is a public issue.

qa.q: A country has 50 million employees, and 15 million are unemployed. What percentage are unemployed?
qa.e: 15 ÷ 50 × 100 = 30%. Mills used this kind of figure to show unemployment as a public issue.

qa.q: Why does sociology treat homelessness as more than a personal hardship?
qa.a: It is linked to lack of jobs and rural-urban migration
qa.e: Many homeless people move to cities seeking work; housing shortages and low wages are structural causes.

qa.q: Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana-Gramin is an example of:
qa.a: A state response to a public issue of housing
qa.e: The state treats housing shortage as a public issue and runs schemes to address it.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): War is a public issue in Mills' sense.
Reason (R): War changes the lives of vast numbers of people through forces far beyond any one person's control.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; war is a public issue precisely because its causes and effects lie in large-scale structures.

qa.q: Case: Sunita's father lost his job when the mill in their town shut down along with three others. Using the sociological imagination, Sunita should see this as:
qa.a: Part of a wider change in industry affecting many families
qa.e: Several mills closing points to a structural change; her family's trouble is linked to a public issue.

qa.q: Which statement about belonging to 'a society' is correct?
qa.a: A person belongs to several societies, and context decides which matters
qa.e: People belong to nation, language, region, religion and other groupings at once.

qa.q: India's plurality refers to:
qa.a: The coexistence of many groups, traditions and ways of life
qa.e: Plurality means diversity of groups, languages, traditions, and village and city life.

qa.q: Sociologically, inequality means:
qa.a: Unequal access of groups to resources such as wealth, education, health and power
qa.e: Inequality is structured unequal access to valued resources and respect.

qa.q: The idea that inequality has many dimensions beyond income is associated with:
qa.a: Amartya Sen
qa.e: Sen argued that well-being includes health, education and freedoms, not only income.

qa.q: District A has 90% households with toilets and District B has 45%. Access in A is how many times that in B?
qa.e: 90 ÷ 45 = 2, so A has double the access: a clear inequality indicator.

qa.q: Case: In a village, a Dalit man is served tea in a separate cup at a tea stall. Sociologically, this shows:
qa.a: Caste-based discrimination in everyday life
qa.e: Separate treatment on the basis of caste denies equal respect; it is discrimination and is unlawful.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Inequality exists within societies as well as between them.
Reason (R): All members of a society have exactly equal access to resources.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: A is true; R is false, because groups within a society differ in access to wealth, education and power.

qa.q: Which is the best indicator of inequality from a health survey?
qa.a: Percentage of households with access to safe sanitation
qa.e: Access to basic services like sanitation varies across groups and shows inequality.

qa.q: Sociology is best defined as:
qa.a: The systematic study of human social life, groups and societies
qa.e: Sociology systematically studies social life, including our own behaviour as social beings.

qa.q: How does sociology differ from philosophical and religious reflection on society?
qa.a: It studies how society actually works, using evidence
qa.e: Sociology is empirical and describes reality rather than prescribing ideals.

qa.q: Peter Berger's comparison of the sociologist to a spy stresses that the sociologist should:
qa.a: Report what is observed without bias
qa.e: Like a spy reporting terrain, a sociologist must describe reality accurately.

qa.q: Sociology is called scientific mainly because:
qa.a: It is bound by rules of evidence that others can check
qa.e: Its claims must be backed by evidence and open to checking.

qa.q: A study that measures caste-wise literacy rates across 600 districts uses mainly:
qa.a: Quantitative methods
qa.e: Measuring rates over many units is quantitative, numerical work.

qa.q: Which pair names a real methodological debate within sociology?
qa.a: Natural-science model versus interpretive model
qa.e: Sociologists debate whether to study society like nature or to interpret meanings.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Sociologists themselves decide how their findings must be used by the government.
Reason (R): How knowledge is used is not itself a sociological question.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: findings can be used in different ways by different users. R is true.

qa.q: Case: A researcher lives in a fishing village for a year, joining daily life and recording people's own explanations. Her approach is best called:
qa.a: Qualitative and interpretive
qa.e: Long observation and attention to meanings is a qualitative, interpretive approach.

qa.q: 'Some people are poor because they are lazy.' This is an example of:
qa.a: An individualistic common-sense explanation
qa.e: It blames the individual and ignores social causes.

qa.q: A sociological explanation of poverty would stress:
qa.a: Class structure, irregular work and low wages
qa.e: Sociology links poverty to the structure of work and resources.

qa.q: Why is common sense called 'unreflective'?
qa.a: It does not question its own origins or assumptions
qa.e: Common sense takes ideas for granted; sociology asks 'is this really so?'

qa.q: A naturalistic explanation says that a social pattern is:
qa.a: Natural or inborn and so cannot change
qa.e: Naturalistic explanations treat social facts as given by nature.

qa.q: Case: After the Kargil war, compensation to some widows led families to press them to marry the deceased husband's brother. This example shows that sociology:
qa.a: Reveals unexpected links between policy, property and kinship
qa.e: A well-meant payment interacted with patrilineal ideas of property in unforeseen ways.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Sociology often questions common-sense beliefs.
Reason (R): Sociology asks 'is this really so?' and tests beliefs against evidence.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; the habit of testing beliefs against evidence is why sociology questions common sense.

qa.q: Which question is typically sociological rather than common-sense?
qa.a: Why do certain groups have higher dropout rates than others?
qa.e: It looks for patterns across groups and their social causes.

qa.q: Under patriliny, descent and property pass through:
qa.a: The male line
qa.e: Patrilineal systems trace descent and inheritance through men.

qa.q: Early sociology borrowed the idea of comparing society to a living organism from:
qa.a: Theories of natural evolution
qa.e: Darwin's evolutionary ideas inspired the view of society as an organism with functioning parts.

qa.q: In the organic analogy, the parts of society are seen as:
qa.a: Performing functions for the whole
qa.e: Like organs in a body, institutions were thought to serve the whole society.

qa.q: Which was a key source of information about non-Western societies for early sociology?
qa.a: Travellers' accounts and colonial administrators' reports
qa.e: Before modern fieldwork, these accounts were the main sources on 'other' societies.

qa.q: Which is the correct order of the classic stages of society?
qa.a: Hunting-gathering, pastoral, agrarian, industrial
qa.e: Early thinkers placed hunting-gathering first and industrial society last.

qa.q: What was a major bias in early stage theories of society?
qa.a: Western industrial society was assumed to be the most advanced
qa.e: They ranked societies with the West at the top.

qa.q: Which group of thinkers is linked with ideas of social evolution and stages?
qa.a: Comte, Marx and Spencer
qa.e: Comte, Marx and Spencer each proposed theories of how societies progress through stages.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Colonial reports were an important source of information about 'other' societies for early sociologists.
Reason (R): Colonial administrators needed knowledge about the people they ruled.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true; administrative needs led to such reports, which sociologists then used.

qa.q: Calling some societies 'primitive' and the West 'advanced' is now criticised because it:
qa.a: Ranks diverse societies using one society's standards
qa.e: Ranking others by Western standards is a biased, Eurocentric assumption.

qa.q: The Enlightenment is best associated with:
qa.a: Reason, individualism and scientific method applied to human affairs
qa.e: It promoted using reason and science to understand society as well as nature.

qa.q: Who is regarded as the founder of sociology?
qa.a: Auguste Comte
qa.e: Comte, a French scholar, is widely regarded as the founder of sociology.

qa.q: Comte believed that sociology would:
qa.a: Contribute to the welfare of humanity
qa.e: He saw sociology as a science that could improve human life.

qa.q: The new view of poverty that emerged with modern thought was that poverty is:
qa.a: A social problem that can be studied and tackled
qa.e: Poverty came to be treated as a 'social problem' with social causes.

qa.q: Collecting facts about the living conditions of people in a city is called a:
qa.a: Social survey
qa.e: Social surveys were an early empirical method of sociology.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The Enlightenment helped create the conditions for sociology.
Reason (R): It encouraged applying reason and the scientific method to the study of human society.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; applying reason and science to society is exactly what made a science of society possible.

qa.q: Which idea would an Enlightenment thinker most likely reject?
qa.a: Social customs should never be questioned
qa.e: The Enlightenment encouraged questioning tradition through reason.

qa.q: Case: A state government surveys households to find which villages lack drinking water before planning pipelines. This continues which early sociological tradition?
qa.a: Social surveys of social problems
qa.e: Measuring living conditions to address problems is the social-survey tradition.

qa.q: The Industrial Revolution was centred in:
qa.a: England
qa.e: Industrialisation began and was centred in England.

qa.q: Which feature best defines capitalism?
qa.a: Private ownership of the means of production, run for profit
qa.e: Capitalism is market enterprise based on private ownership and profit.

qa.q: Under capitalism, human labour:
qa.a: Becomes a commodity sold for wages
qa.e: Workers sell their capacity to work in the labour market.

qa.q: Pre-industrial European society was mainly:
qa.a: Village-based, hierarchical and close-knit
qa.e: Peasants, artisans and landlords lived in close, ranked village communities.

qa.q: The 'degradation of labour' during industrialisation refers to:
qa.a: Workers cut off from guild, village and family, reduced to wage labour
qa.e: Industrial work stripped workers of older ties and control over their work.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): In industrial capitalism, workers depend on wages.
Reason (R): Most workers do not own the means of production.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; since workers lack means of production, they must sell labour for wages.

qa.q: Case: A handloom weaver who once sold cloth to village buyers now works shifts in a power-loom factory owned by a businessman. This change best illustrates:
qa.a: The shift to industrial capitalism
qa.e: Private ownership, wage work and market production mark capitalism.

qa.q: Which term means 'market enterprise based on private ownership of the means of production'?
qa.a: Capitalism
qa.e: That is the glossary definition of capitalism.

qa.q: Which of these was a typical feature of early industrial cities?
qa.a: Crowded slums and pollution
qa.e: Rapid factory growth produced overcrowding, slums and pollution.

qa.q: How did Marx view factory production?
qa.a: As oppressive, yet potentially liberating through collective organisation
qa.e: Gathering workers together made them exploited but also able to unite.

qa.q: The phrase 'time is money' reflects:
qa.a: Work organised and paid by clock time
qa.e: Industrial work measured labour in hours and minutes.

qa.q: While Britain urbanised rapidly during industrialisation, colonial India saw:
qa.a: Many people pushed back into agriculture
qa.e: Decline of traditional industry pushed Indians into farming.

qa.q: 'Dialectic' in sociology refers to:
qa.a: The interplay of opposing social forces
qa.e: For example, social constraint versus individual will.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Factory work introduced a strict sense of clock time.
Reason (R): Factory machines and shifts needed workers to start and stop together at set hours.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; coordinated machine production required clock discipline.

qa.q: Case: In 1850, a weaver leaves his village workshop for a Manchester mill. Which change is he most likely to face?
qa.a: Working fixed hours on one repeated task
qa.e: Mechanical division of labour and clock time defined factory work.

qa.q: The mechanical division of labour in factories meant that each worker:
qa.a: Performed a small, repetitive part of production
qa.e: Production was broken into simple repeated tasks.

qa.q: Why should Indian students study the growth of sociology in Europe?
qa.a: Because issues like urbanisation and capitalism also shaped India
qa.e: India's history is entangled with European capitalism and colonialism.

qa.q: Indentured Indian labourers were taken to which set of places?
qa.a: Fiji, Surinam, the West Indies and Mauritius
qa.e: These plantation economies drew heavily on indentured Indian labour.

qa.q: The global spread of Western capitalism involved:
qa.a: Slavery of Africans and indentured labour from India
qa.e: Plantation economies relied on enslaved and indentured workers.

qa.q: R.K. Laxman's account of Mauritius highlights:
qa.a: Its mixed population shaped by colonial history
qa.e: Laxman noted how colonial labour flows created a diverse population.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): India's social history cannot be fully understood without studying British capitalism.
Reason (R): India's history is entangled with British capitalism and colonialism.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; the entanglement is the reason the European story is needed.

qa.q: Case: Large numbers of Indians live in Fiji and Trinidad. A sociologist would trace this mainly to:
qa.a: Colonial indentured labour for plantations
qa.e: Most of these communities descend from indentured plantation workers.

qa.q: Which statement is correct?
qa.a: Urbanisation and factory production concern all modern societies
qa.e: These are general features of modern society.

qa.q: The system under which Indian workers signed contracts to work for fixed years on overseas plantations is called:
qa.a: Indentured labour
qa.e: Indenture meant contracted labour for a fixed term, often under harsh conditions.

qa.q: Why must Western sociology be read in the light of colonial experience?
qa.a: Because colonialism was integral to modern capitalism
qa.e: Capitalism grew through colonies' resources, markets and labour.

qa.q: Marx's observation about India concerned:
qa.a: The ruin of handloom weavers by cheap English cloth
qa.e: Cheap machine-made imports destroyed handloom livelihoods.

qa.q: The colonial image of the Indian village as unchanging was:
qa.a: Wrong, since villages had a history and kept changing
qa.e: Research showed Indian villages were dynamic.

qa.q: Who remarked that in a diverse society like India 'the other' lives next door?
qa.a: M.N. Srinivas
qa.e: Srinivas pointed out that Indian researchers study groups very close to them.

qa.q: In the West, social anthropology traditionally studied:
qa.a: Simple, small-scale societies
qa.e: Sociology took modern societies, anthropology the 'simple' ones.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): In India, the boundary between sociology and social anthropology was blurred.
Reason (R): India contains villages and cities, castes and tribes, tradition and modernity side by side.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; India's mix of forms is why the boundary blurred.

qa.q: Which is the correct sequence in the widening focus of Indian social anthropology?
qa.a: 'Primitive' peoples, then peasants and castes, then classes and industry
qa.e: The focus broadened over time from tribes to the whole of Indian society.

qa.q: Case: A Delhi researcher studies a caste community living in the same city. This illustrates which idea?
qa.a: 'The other' lives next door in India
qa.e: The studied group is close at hand, as Srinivas noted.

qa.q: Which pair shows the full scope of sociology?
qa.a: A shopkeeper-customer chat and global economic processes
qa.e: Sociology ranges from micro interactions to macro and global processes.

qa.q: Sociology is distinguished from other social sciences mainly by:
qa.a: How it studies, i.e. its perspective and methods
qa.e: Many topics overlap; the sociological perspective marks the difference.

qa.q: Feminist theory argues for:
qa.a: Interdisciplinary work across social sciences
qa.e: Gender issues cut across economics, politics and sociology.

qa.q: Feminist economists have stressed the importance of:
qa.a: Counting unpaid domestic work
qa.e: Unpaid household and care work is real economic work that standard measures miss.

qa.q: A sociologist studying the economy would focus most on:
qa.a: The norms, values and social relations shaping economic behaviour
qa.e: Sociology places economic behaviour in its social setting.

qa.q: Who urged that economists count all the social costs of economic decisions?
qa.a: Pierre Bourdieu
qa.e: Bourdieu criticised narrow economic accounting that ignores social costs.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Advertising is of interest to sociologists, not only to economists.
Reason (R): Advertisements often sell lifestyles, status and identities along with products.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; because ads trade on culture and status, consumption is a sociological topic.

qa.q: Case: A family buys a costly phone mainly so that relatives see them as 'modern'. This best shows:
qa.a: Consumption shaped by status and culture
qa.e: Buying to display status is culturally shaped economic behaviour.

qa.q: Political sociology mainly studies:
qa.a: Actual political behaviour such as voting, parties and decision-making
qa.e: It studies how politics works in practice in society.

qa.q: Which thinker is cited as a classic political sociologist?
qa.a: Max Weber
qa.e: Weber's work on power, authority and bureaucracy is political sociology.

qa.q: How does sociology differ from history in its approach?
qa.a: Sociology studies the recent past and generalises; history details concrete past events
qa.e: Historians reconstruct particular events; sociologists abstract patterns.

qa.q: Durkheim's study of suicide is important because it showed that suicide rates:
qa.a: Are social facts linked to social integration
qa.e: Rates vary with social bonds and are patterned across groups.

qa.q: The field that bridges psychology and sociology is:
qa.a: Social psychology
qa.e: Social psychology studies how individuals behave in social settings.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Social history has brought history and sociology closer.
Reason (R): Social history studies social patterns such as caste, gender and everyday life over time.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; by studying social patterns, social history overlaps with sociology.

qa.q: Case: A researcher compares women's participation in panchayat elections across states before and after reservation. This research belongs most clearly to:
qa.a: Political sociology
qa.e: It studies gender in actual political participation.

qa.q: Which is a good example of disciplines borrowing from each other?
qa.a: A historian using the concept of 'class' to study a peasant revolt
qa.e: Concepts and data move across disciplines.

qa.q: Which of these is NOT a branch of anthropology?
qa.a: Econometrics
qa.e: Anthropology's branches include physical, social/cultural, archaeology and linguistics; econometrics is economics.

qa.q: Ethnography refers to:
qa.a: A detailed description of a community's way of life based on fieldwork
qa.e: Ethnographers observe and describe life in depth through long fieldwork.

qa.q: Traditionally, sociology relied more than anthropology on:
qa.a: Surveys and questionnaires
qa.e: Sociology used surveys and statistics; anthropology used long fieldwork.

qa.q: A major critique of Western anthropology is that:
qa.a: It had an unequal relationship with the 'natives'
qa.e: Colonial power shaped who studied whom.

qa.q: Colonialism undermined the idea that 'simple' societies were:
qa.a: Isolated and bounded
qa.e: Colonial contact showed these societies were connected to wider processes.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Indian sociology borrows from both sociology and social anthropology.
Reason (R): India combines tradition and modernity, village and city, caste and tribe, class and community.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; India's mixed social reality is why both traditions are needed.

qa.q: Case: A researcher spends 14 months in a Gond village learning the language and recording rituals. Her method is mainly:
qa.a: Anthropological fieldwork and ethnography
qa.e: Long residence and detailed description define ethnography.

qa.q: Why are Santhal tea workers in Assam a good case for combining anthropology and sociology?
qa.a: They are both a community with traditions and a wage-labour class
qa.e: Their lives involve community culture and plantation labour relations.

qa.q: Why does sociology need special terms and concepts?
qa.a: Because everyday words are vague and sociology needs precise meanings
qa.e: Precise concepts let sociologists observe, compare and theorise reliably.

qa.q: Which is NOT a function of sociological concepts?
qa.a: Replacing the need for evidence
qa.e: Concepts help organise and compare evidence; they do not replace it.

qa.q: The statement 'concepts carry the stamp of their social context' means:
qa.a: Concepts reflect the debates and conditions in which they arose
qa.e: For example, 'class' emerged from debates about industrial capitalism.

qa.q: A researcher defines 'joint family' differently in two surveys. The main problem is:
qa.a: The findings cannot be compared reliably
qa.e: Without consistent concepts, comparison breaks down.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Sociologists use precise concepts.
Reason (R): Everyday terms such as 'group' have many loose meanings.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; the looseness of everyday terms is why precision is needed.

qa.q: The concept of 'class' in sociology emerged mainly from debates about:
qa.a: Industrial capitalism
qa.e: Thinkers like Marx developed class to analyse capitalist society.

qa.q: Case: Two students argue whether a crowd at a cricket match is a 'group'. What would settle it in sociology?
qa.a: A clear definition of a social group
qa.e: A precise concept tells us which features a group must have.

qa.q: Concepts help sociologists compare societies because they:
qa.a: Give a common, defined yardstick across cases
qa.e: A shared definition allows like-for-like comparison.

qa.q: The functionalist perspective views society as:
qa.a: A system of interdependent parts that maintain order
qa.e: Functionalists stress interdependence, functions and stability.

qa.q: The conflict perspective emphasises:
qa.a: Inequality, power and competition for scarce resources
qa.e: Conflict theorists see dominant groups shaping society to their interest.

qa.q: Which is an example of a macro-level study?
qa.a: How globalisation changes employment patterns in India
qa.e: Macro studies large structures and processes.

qa.q: A study of how a shopkeeper and customer bargain is at the:
qa.a: Micro level
qa.e: Face-to-face interaction is micro-level.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The functionalist and conflict perspectives can study the same institution.
Reason (R): Each perspective highlights different aspects, such as order or inequality.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; because they highlight different aspects, both can be applied to one institution.

qa.q: Which statement best describes the individual-society relationship in sociology?
qa.a: Individuals shape society and are also shaped by it
qa.e: Sociology treats this as a two-way, interlinked duality.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): A conflict theorist sees the education system as always serving all groups equally.
Reason (R): The conflict perspective focuses on inequality and power.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: a conflict theorist sees institutions as often favouring dominant groups. R is true.

qa.q: Case: A sociologist argues that festivals bring a village together and reinforce shared values. Which perspective is this?
qa.a: Functionalist
qa.e: Stressing integration and shared values is functionalist.

qa.q: Which feature is essential to a social group?
qa.a: Regular interaction with a shared sense of belonging
qa.e: Groups have continuity, shared norms and goals, and a 'we' feeling.

qa.q: Passengers waiting together on a railway platform are an example of:
qa.a: An aggregate
qa.e: They are together in space but lack lasting connection.

qa.q: Which is an example of a quasi-group?
qa.a: A social class
qa.e: A quasi-group lacks structure, and members may be unaware of the grouping.

qa.q: A quasi-group can turn into a social group when its members:
qa.a: Begin to interact, organise and develop common goals
qa.e: Organisation and shared goals transform a quasi-group.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): A cinema audience is not a social group.
Reason (R): Members of the audience do not interact in a sustained, structured way.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; the lack of sustained interaction is why it is only an aggregate.

qa.q: Case: Flood victims in a relief camp form a committee, choose leaders and meet daily to demand aid. They have become:
qa.a: A social group
qa.e: They now interact regularly with structure and shared goals.

qa.q: Which pair is correctly matched?
qa.a: Age group: quasi-group
qa.e: Age categories lack organisation, so they are quasi-groups.

qa.q: Why is a social class called a quasi-group?
qa.a: It lacks organisation and members may be unaware of it
qa.e: Classes share position but are not necessarily organised.

qa.q: Who introduced the concept of the primary group?
qa.a: C.H. Cooley
qa.e: Cooley described primary groups as intimate face-to-face associations.

qa.q: Which is a feature of a primary group?
qa.a: Intimate, face-to-face, lasting relationships
qa.e: Primary groups involve whole-person, close ties.

qa.q: Which is an example of a secondary group?
qa.a: A trade union
qa.e: Unions are formal, goal-oriented and impersonal.

qa.q: Tönnies' 'Gesellschaft' refers to:
qa.a: Society or association with impersonal, contractual ties
qa.e: Gesellschaft relations are impersonal and goal-based.

qa.q: 'Gemeinschaft' is best translated as:
qa.a: Community
qa.e: Gemeinschaft means community with personal, emotional ties.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): People in a secondary group usually relate to each other through specific roles.
Reason (R): Secondary groups are large and goal-oriented.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; size and goal-orientation make relations role-specific.

qa.q: Case: Ankit chats with the bank cashier only about his deposit, but shares all his worries with his cousin. The bank and his cousin's family represent:
qa.a: Secondary and primary relationships respectively
qa.e: The bank relation is role-specific (secondary); the family relation is intimate (primary).

qa.q:
Assertion (A): A political party is a secondary group.
Reason (R): Political parties are small, intimate, face-to-face groups.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: A is true. R is false: parties are large, formal and goal-oriented, which is why they are secondary groups.

qa.q: The in-group and out-group distinction is associated with:
qa.a: W.G. Sumner
qa.e: Sumner distinguished 'we' groups from 'they' groups.

qa.q: A reference group is one that:
qa.a: We use as a standard and aspire to imitate
qa.e: We judge ourselves by its standards, whether or not we belong.

qa.q: Colonial-era middle-class Indians copying British dress and speech illustrates:
qa.a: The British as a reference group
qa.e: They modelled their behaviour on the British.

qa.q: A peer group is best described as:
qa.a: A primary group of people of similar age or status
qa.e: Peers share age or status and interact closely.

qa.q: Case: Students from Delhi and Chennai argue about whose food is better, but cheer together for the Indian team abroad. This shows that:
qa.a: In-group boundaries change with context
qa.e: The 'we' expands from region to nation depending on the situation.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Peer pressure can lead a teenager to start a habit only because friends do it.
Reason (R): Peer groups exert social influence to make members conform.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; the conforming influence of peers is what peer pressure is.

qa.q: Which is NOT an example of a reference group in action?
qa.a: A child obeying traffic signals because of a fine
qa.e: Obeying due to a fine is formal control, not imitation of a reference group.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): An out-group is always made of people from another country.
Reason (R): Out-groups are defined by a sense of 'they' in a given context.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: an out-group can be another school, team or locality. R is true.

qa.q: Social stratification refers to:
qa.a: Structured, persistent inequality between groups
qa.e: It is patterned inequality built into society and lasting over time.

qa.q: Which of the following is the most open system of stratification?
qa.a: Class
qa.e: Class allows mobility based on economic position.

qa.q: The estate system is associated mainly with:
qa.a: Feudal Europe
qa.e: Medieval Europe had clergy, nobility and commoners as estates.

qa.q: 'Life chances' means:
qa.a: The opportunities and rewards linked to social position
qa.e: Position shapes access to health, education and income.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Stratification persists across generations.
Reason (R): Families pass on advantages and disadvantages to their children.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; inheritance of advantage is why stratification persists.

qa.q: Which statement correctly describes stratification?
qa.a: It is a social feature that ranks groups by access to rewards
qa.e: It is social, group-based and found in all known complex societies.

qa.q: Case: Two equally bright students; one from an affluent family gets private tutors and internships, the other from a poor family leaves school to work. A sociologist would explain this through:
qa.a: Differences in life chances due to stratification
qa.e: Their social positions give unequal opportunities.

qa.q: A system where a person's position is fixed for life with almost no mobility is called:
qa.a: Closed
qa.e: Closed systems, like slavery or traditional caste, allow little movement.

qa.q: Which feature belongs to caste as a system of stratification?
qa.a: Status ascribed at birth
qa.e: Caste membership is determined by birth.

qa.q: Which feature belongs to class?
qa.a: It is based on wealth, income and occupation
qa.e: Class is an economic form of stratification.

qa.q: Traditional caste ranking was based on ideas of:
qa.a: Purity and pollution
qa.e: Castes were ranked by ritual purity.

qa.q: Why is class called an 'open' system?
qa.a: Individuals can move up or down through achievement
qa.e: Mobility through education or occupation is possible.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Gender is a cross-cutting dimension of inequality.
Reason (R): Women within the same caste or class can face additional disadvantages compared to men.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; added disadvantages within caste and class are what make gender cross-cutting.

qa.q: Which article of the Indian Constitution abolishes untouchability?
qa.a: Article 17
qa.e: Article 17 abolishes untouchability and forbids its practice.

qa.q: Case: In a city, a woman software engineer and a man in the same company with the same qualifications get different promotions. Sociologists would look at:
qa.a: Gender as a dimension of inequality within class
qa.e: Same class position, yet gender produces a difference.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Caste status is ascribed at birth.
Reason (R): Caste has traditionally allowed high social mobility.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: A is true. R is false: because status was fixed by birth, traditional caste allowed little mobility.

qa.q: Status in sociology refers to:
qa.a: A socially defined position with rights and duties
qa.e: Status is a position such as teacher or mother.

qa.q: Which is an achieved status?
qa.a: Doctor
qa.e: Becoming a doctor requires effort and qualification.

qa.q: Which is an ascribed status?
qa.a: Being born into a particular kin group
qa.e: Kinship position is given by birth.

qa.q: 'Status is occupied, role is played' means:
qa.a: A role is the behaviour expected of the position one holds
qa.e: Role is the dynamic, behavioural side of status.

qa.q: The concept of 'role set' was given by:
qa.a: Robert K. Merton
qa.e: Merton described the set of role relations linked to one status.

qa.q: A school teacher interacting with students, parents, the principal and other teachers illustrates:
qa.a: Role set
qa.e: These are many role relations attached to one status, teacher.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Status also has the meaning of prestige.
Reason (R): Societies rank occupations and positions differently in esteem.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; because positions are ranked in esteem, status also means prestige.

qa.q: Case: Rahul is a son, a student, a cricket captain and a nephew. How many statuses are mentioned?
qa.e: Son, student, captain and nephew are four statuses.

qa.q: Role conflict refers to:
qa.a: Clashing expectations from different statuses or roles
qa.e: It occurs when role demands are incompatible.

qa.q: Which is an example of role stereotyping?
qa.a: Assuming that only women should be nurses
qa.e: It fixes a role to a gender.

qa.q: Case: Inspector Rao must arrest his own cousin. He faces:
qa.a: Role conflict
qa.e: His duties as officer clash with expectations as a relative.

qa.q: The statement 'roles are contested and change with society' is shown by:
qa.a: Women entering professions once closed to them
qa.e: Changing gender roles show roles are social.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Role stereotyping limits both men and women.
Reason (R): It fixes roles to groups regardless of individual ability or choice.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; because roles are fixed by group, both genders are restricted.

qa.q: A man who leaves his job to take care of his children challenges which stereotype?
qa.a: Men as breadwinners
qa.e: He breaks the expectation that men must earn while women care.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Role conflict can only arise between two different statuses.
Reason (R): A single status can carry incompatible expectations from different people.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: conflict can also arise within one status (e.g. a teacher expected to be both strict and friendly). R is true.

qa.q: Which statement about statuses and roles is correct?
qa.a: They are socially defined and can change
qa.e: Roles vary across societies and over time.

qa.q: Social control refers to:
qa.a: Ways society regulates behaviour to maintain order
qa.e: It includes formal and informal regulation of behaviour.

qa.q: Which is an example of formal social control?
qa.a: A court sentencing a thief
qa.e: Courts are official, codified agencies.

qa.q: Which is an example of informal social control?
qa.a: Ridicule by classmates
qa.e: Ridicule is personal and unofficial.

qa.q: The conflict view sees social control as:
qa.a: A means for dominant groups to keep their power
qa.e: Conflict theorists ask whose interests control serves.

qa.q: The functionalist view sees social control as:
qa.a: Necessary for order and stability
qa.e: Functionalists see control maintaining social order.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Informal social control can be very powerful even without laws.
Reason (R): People care about the approval of family, friends and community.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; the desire for approval gives informal control its force.

qa.q: Case: In a housing society, residents who park badly find notes stuck on their cars by neighbours and are also fined under society bye-laws. These are examples of:
qa.a: Informal and formal control respectively
qa.e: Notes from neighbours are informal; bye-law fines are formal.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Formal social control is uncodified.
Reason (R): Formal control works through official agencies like the police and courts.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: formal control is codified (written laws and rules). R is true.

qa.q: A positive sanction is:
qa.a: A reward for conforming behaviour
qa.e: Positive sanctions encourage behaviour through rewards.

qa.q: Which is a negative sanction?
qa.a: A fine for breaking a traffic rule
qa.e: Fines punish violations.

qa.q: Deviance refers to:
qa.a: Behaviour departing from accepted norms
qa.e: Deviance is broader than crime and depends on norms.

qa.q: Why is deviance said to be relative?
qa.a: Because norms differ across societies and change over time
qa.e: Something deviant in one setting may be normal in another.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Sanctions help maintain social order.
Reason (R): Sanctions reward conformity and punish violations of norms.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; by rewarding and punishing, sanctions keep behaviour in line with norms.

qa.q: Case: In one company, employees who come late get a warning letter, and those who meet targets get a bonus. These are:
qa.a: A negative and a positive sanction
qa.e: A warning punishes; a bonus rewards.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Every act of deviance is a crime.
Reason (R): Crime is a breach of law, while deviance is any departure from norms.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: deviance is broader; many deviant acts (e.g. odd dress) break no law. R is true.

qa.q: A student is cheered by classmates for standing up to a bully. This is an example of:
qa.a: An informal positive sanction
qa.e: Cheering by peers is unofficial and rewarding.

qa.q: A social institution is best defined as:
qa.a: A lasting pattern of norms, values and roles meeting social needs
qa.e: Institutions are enduring rule-governed patterns, not buildings.

qa.q: Which pair correctly shows the double nature of institutions?
qa.a: They constrain and enable individuals
qa.e: Institutions impose limits but also create opportunities.

qa.q: Which is an example of a formal institution?
qa.a: The legal system
qa.e: The legal system is codified and official.

qa.q: According to the conflict perspective, institutions:
qa.a: Tend to favour dominant groups
qa.e: Conflict theorists see institutions reproducing inequality.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Changes in the economy can alter family life.
Reason (R): Micro and macro institutions are interlinked.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; because institutions are interlinked, economic change affects families.

qa.q: Case: A new law raises the minimum age of marriage, and families delay weddings. This shows:
qa.a: Interlinking of the state (macro) with the family (micro)
qa.e: A state decision changes family practice.

qa.q: The functionalist view of institutions stresses that they:
qa.a: Meet the needs of society and maintain stability
qa.e: Functionalists see institutions as serving social needs.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Social institutions only restrict people.
Reason (R): Institutions also open up opportunities, such as education leading to jobs.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: institutions also enable. R is true.

qa.q: A nuclear family consists of:
qa.a: One set of parents and their children
qa.e: That is the definition of a nuclear family.

qa.q: Which feature identifies an extended (joint) family?
qa.a: More than one couple, often across generations, living together
qa.e: Extended families include several couples and generations.

qa.q: Functionalist sociologists argued that the nuclear family is suited to industrial society because it is:
qa.a: Small and mobile
qa.e: Industrial jobs require families to move, which is easier for small units.

qa.q: Which statement is a valid critique of the 'nuclear family = modern' idea?
qa.a: Joint families have persisted and adapted in modern India
qa.e: Family forms change in many directions, not just toward the nuclear.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Functionalists argued that the nuclear family suits industrial society.
Reason (R): Industrial jobs often require workers to move from place to place.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; the need for mobility is exactly why functionalists saw the small nuclear family as suited to industry.

qa.q: Case: Raju's family includes his parents, his uncle, his uncle's wife and their children, all sharing a kitchen. The family type is:
qa.a: Joint/extended
qa.e: More than one couple share a household.

qa.q: A family is defined as a group in which:
qa.a: Members are linked by kin ties and adults care for children
qa.e: Kin ties and responsibility for children define family.

qa.q: Which of these is generally truer of a nuclear family than a joint family?
qa.a: It can move more easily for jobs
qa.e: Small size makes mobility easier.

qa.q: The fall in marriage rates in former East Germany after unification shows that:
qa.a: Family is affected by changes in economy and state
qa.e: Withdrawal of state support and insecurity reduced marriages.

qa.q: The child sex ratio fell from 945 to 927 between 1991 and 2001. What was the fall?
qa.e: 945 − 927 = 18 girls per 1,000 boys.

qa.q: A declining child sex ratio mainly indicates:
qa.a: Son preference and discrimination against girls
qa.e: Fewer girls per 1,000 boys points to discrimination.

qa.q: The child sex ratio is measured as:
qa.a: Number of girls per 1,000 boys aged 0–6
qa.e: In India it is girls per 1,000 boys in the 0–6 age group.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Family life is shaped by other institutions.
Reason (R): The family is linked with the economy, polity and culture.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; the links explain why family life is shaped by other institutions.

qa.q: Case: In a town, many young people postpone marriage after a big factory shuts down. A sociologist would explain this by:
qa.a: Economic insecurity affecting family decisions
qa.e: Economic change shapes family formation.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Son preference is a feature found only among poor families.
Reason (R): Son preference is linked to ideas about inheritance and old-age support.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: son preference cuts across classes. R is true.

qa.q: Which law prohibits sex selection in India?
qa.a: The PCPNDT Act
qa.e: The Pre-Conception and Pre-Natal Diagnostic Techniques Act bans sex selection.

qa.q: In patrilocal residence, a newly married couple lives with:
qa.a: The husband's family
qa.e: Patri- refers to the father's/husband's side.

qa.q: Matrilineal descent means that:
qa.a: Property and descent pass from mother to daughter
qa.e: Matriliny concerns descent and inheritance.

qa.q: Which community is a well-known example of matriliny in India?
