qa.a: The Khasi of Meghalaya
qa.e: The Khasi trace descent through women.

qa.q: A patriarchal family is one where:
qa.a: Men exercise authority and dominance
qa.e: Patriarchy refers to male authority.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Matriarchy is considered more a theoretical than an empirical concept.
Reason (R): There is little historical evidence of societies where women held general dominance.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; the lack of evidence is why matriarchy is seen as theoretical.

qa.q: Case: In a family, the couple lives with the wife's parents. The residence rule is:
qa.a: Matrilocal
qa.e: Living with the wife's family is matrilocal.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): In a matrilineal society, authority always rests with women.
Reason (R): In many matrilineal societies, the mother's brother holds authority.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false; R is true and shows that matriliny does not mean women hold authority.

qa.q: Which three bases are used to classify family forms in the chapter?
qa.a: Residence, descent and authority
qa.e: Families are classified by where couples live, how descent runs and who holds authority.

qa.q: Polygyny refers to:
qa.a: One man married to two or more women at the same time
qa.e: Gyn- refers to women: many wives.

qa.q: Polyandry refers to:
qa.a: One woman married to two or more men at once
qa.e: Andr- refers to men: many husbands.

qa.q: Serial monogamy means:
qa.a: One spouse at a time, remarrying after death or divorce
qa.e: It is still monogamy, one spouse at a time.

qa.q: Fraternal polyandry has been linked with:
qa.a: Scarce land and harsh economic conditions
qa.e: Brothers sharing a wife keeps scarce land undivided.

qa.q: Polygyny and polyandry are both types of:
qa.a: Polygamy
qa.e: Both involve more than one spouse at once.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): A widower who remarries is practising serial monogamy.
Reason (R): Polygamy means having only one spouse at a time.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: A is true: he has one spouse at a time. R is false: polygamy means more than one spouse at the same time.

qa.q: Case: In a Himalayan village with little farmland, two brothers share one wife so the family land is not split. This is:
qa.a: Fraternal polyandry
qa.e: Brothers jointly married to one wife is fraternal polyandry.

qa.q: Marriage is described as a 'socially sanctioned' union because:
qa.a: Society and often law recognise it with rights and duties
qa.e: Social and legal recognition makes it an institution.

qa.q: Endogamy is the rule of marrying:
qa.a: Within a defined group such as caste
qa.e: Endo = within.

qa.q: Exogamy is the rule of marrying:
qa.a: Outside a defined group such as clan or village
qa.e: Exo = outside.

qa.q: A person's mother-in-law is an example of which kind of kin?
qa.a: Affinal
qa.e: In-laws are related through marriage.

qa.q: The family into which a person is born is called the family of:
qa.a: Orientation
qa.e: It orients the child into society.

qa.q: When Raju marries and has children, the new family he forms is his family of:
qa.a: Procreation
qa.e: It is formed through marriage and having children.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Caste endogamy and gotra exogamy can apply to the same marriage.
Reason (R): Endogamy and exogamy apply to different groups.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; since the rules apply to different groups, one can marry within caste but outside gotra.

qa.q: Which is a consanguineal relative?
qa.a: Mother's brother
qa.e: The mother's brother is related by blood.

qa.q: Case: In a north Indian village, a girl cannot marry a boy from the same village even if they are from different families. This rule is:
qa.a: Village exogamy
qa.e: Requiring marriage outside the village is exogamy.

qa.q: Case: Sneha and Arjun met in college and chose each other; their families then met, fixed the date and arranged all the rituals. Sociologically, this shows that:
qa.a: Self-chosen and arranged elements are often mixed in Indian marriages
qa.e: Self-chosen ('love') marriages are increasing, but families often still arrange the wedding; many marriages combine both.

qa.q: Sociologically, work is best defined as:
qa.a: Tasks needing mental and physical effort to produce goods and services
qa.e: Work can be paid or unpaid.

qa.q: Which is an example of unpaid work?
qa.a: Caring for a sick family member at home
qa.e: Care work at home is unpaid but is still work.

qa.q: The informal economy refers to:
qa.a: Work outside regular, regulated employment
qa.e: Informal work lacks regular contracts and protections, but is not necessarily illegal.

qa.q: A complex division of labour means:
qa.a: Tasks are specialised and people depend on each other
qa.e: Specialisation creates interdependence.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Unpaid domestic work is often unrecognised.
Reason (R): It is not paid and is usually not counted in standard economic measures.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; not being paid or counted is why it goes unrecognised.

qa.q: Industrial production changed work mainly by:
qa.a: Separating home from workplace
qa.e: Factories made people work away from home.

qa.q: Case: Leela works as a cook in four homes, with no contract, leave or pension. Her work is part of the:
qa.a: Informal economy
qa.e: Work without contracts or protections is informal.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Most work done by peasants and artisans in pre-industrial times was done away from home in factories.
Reason (R): Industrial production separated the home and the workplace.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: pre-industrial work was largely home- or village-based. R is true; it describes the later industrial change.

qa.q: Scientific management is associated with:
qa.a: F.W. Taylor
qa.e: Taylor broke jobs into timed, simple tasks.

qa.q: Fordism refers to:
qa.a: Mass production of standard goods on assembly lines
qa.e: Ford's car factories symbolised assembly-line mass production.

qa.q: Flexible production is characterised by:
qa.a: Small batches, outsourcing and quick response to demand
qa.e: It replaces rigid mass production with adaptable chains.

qa.q: A global brand gets its clothes stitched by subcontractors in Bangladesh and India. This is an example of:
qa.a: Outsourcing in global production
qa.e: Production tasks are contracted out across countries.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Work has become more insecure for many workers.
Reason (R): Permanent jobs with benefits have declined while contract labour has grown.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; the shift to contract work is the reason for insecurity.

qa.q: Which is a sign of insecurity of work?
qa.a: Short-term contracts without pension or leave
qa.e: Contract jobs lack security and benefits.

qa.q: Case: A worker on an assembly line fixes only car doors, 400 times a day, timed by a supervisor. This shows:
qa.a: Fordism with scientific management
qa.e: Assembly lines (Ford) plus timed tasks (Taylor).

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Globalisation has made flexible production easier.
Reason (R): Improved communication and transport let firms outsource across countries.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; better connections are what make global outsourcing possible.

qa.q: Political institutions are mainly concerned with:
qa.a: The acquisition and distribution of power
qa.e: Politics is about power in society.

qa.q: Power is defined as:
qa.a: The ability to carry out one's will even against resistance
qa.e: This is Weber's definition used in the chapter.

qa.q: Authority is:
qa.a: Power that is accepted as legitimate
qa.e: Authority is legitimate, accepted power.

qa.q: Saying power is a 'fixed quantity' means that:
qa.a: If one person or group has more, others have less
qa.e: Power is held by some to the extent it is not held by others.

qa.q: How is order maintained in stateless societies?
qa.a: Through kinship, age-sets, rituals and cross-cutting ties
qa.e: Without a state, other institutions keep order.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Authority is power that is accepted as legitimate.
Reason (R): Anyone who can force others to obey, even a robber with a gun, has authority.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: A is true. R is false: a robber has power but no legitimacy, so no authority.

qa.q: Case: In a pastoral community without a government, disputes are settled by elders of age-groups and kin. This is an example of:
qa.a: A stateless society
qa.e: Order without a formal state apparatus.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): A judge's ruling is obeyed by most people even when they disagree with it.
Reason (R): The judge's power is seen as legitimate authority.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; legitimacy is why rulings are obeyed.

qa.q: The state is best defined as:
qa.a: A political apparatus ruling a territory, backed by law and force
qa.e: Territory, law and the capacity to use force define a state.

qa.q: Sovereignty means:
qa.a: Undisputed political rule over a territory
qa.e: A sovereign state has supreme authority over its territory.

qa.q: Which of these is a social right?
qa.a: The right to basic welfare such as health care
qa.e: Social rights cover welfare and economic security.

qa.q: The right to vote is a:
qa.a: Political right
qa.e: Political rights are about participation in government.

qa.q: According to the functionalist view, the state:
qa.a: Serves the interests of all sections of society
qa.e: Functionalists see the state as representing society as a whole.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Citizenship rights have expanded over time.
Reason (R): Excluded groups struggled for and won new rights.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; struggles by excluded groups are why rights expanded.

qa.q: Nationalism is best described as:
qa.a: A sense of belonging to a political community
qa.e: It refers to identification with a nation as a political community.

qa.q: Case: A campaign by women's groups leads to a law guaranteeing equal pay for equal work. This shows that:
qa.a: Social movements can expand citizens' rights
qa.e: Struggles of excluded groups widen citizenship.

qa.q: How does the sociological study of religion differ from theology?
qa.a: It is empirical and does not judge which faith is true
qa.e: Sociology studies religion's social aspects without judging truth.

qa.q: Durkheim's distinction in the study of religion is between:
qa.a: The sacred and the profane
qa.e: Sacred things are set apart; profane are ordinary.

qa.q: For Durkheim, the 'sacred' refers to things that are:
qa.a: Set apart and treated with awe and reverence
qa.e: Sacredness comes from social meaning and reverence.

qa.q: Which is NOT a common feature of religion as described sociologically?
qa.a: A written tax code
qa.e: Tax codes belong to the state, not religion.

qa.q: A comparative approach to religion means:
qa.a: Studying religion across different societies and faiths
qa.e: Comparison helps see common and distinct patterns.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Religion is linked with power and stratification.
Reason (R): Religious institutions can be connected with politics and social hierarchy.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; these connections are what link religion to power and stratification.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Sociologists of religion try to decide which religion is true.
Reason (R): The sociological study of religion is non-judgemental.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false; R is true and contradicts A.

qa.q: Case: A researcher studies how a village festival brings different castes together and also where each caste stands during the procession. She is studying:
qa.a: Religion's links with community and stratification
qa.e: She studies social functions and hierarchy, not truth.

qa.q: Weber's 'The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism' argues that:
qa.a: The Calvinist ethic of work and frugality aided capitalism
qa.e: Religious values encouraged saving and reinvestment.

qa.q: In Weber's argument, why did Calvinists save rather than spend?
qa.a: Their ethic rejected luxury and valued frugality
qa.e: Frugality was a religious virtue.

qa.q: Which example shows religion as a force for social change in India?
qa.a: Bhakti saints challenging caste hierarchy
qa.e: Bhakti and reform movements questioned caste and ritual.

qa.q: The secularisation thesis states that:
qa.a: Religion would decline in importance as societies modernise
qa.e: It predicted a decline of religion with modernity.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Religion continues to be important in public life in many modern societies.
Reason (R): The secularisation thesis predicted that religion would decline in modern societies.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true, but R does not explain A; in fact A is evidence that questions the thesis described in R.

qa.q: Religion and gender are linked because:
qa.a: Religious norms often shape women's and men's roles
qa.e: Religious ideas influence gender roles; reform can also challenge them.

qa.q: Case: In a reform movement, a saint invites people of all castes to eat together after prayers. Sociologically this shows:
qa.a: Religion promoting social change
qa.e: Shared meals across castes challenge hierarchy.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Weber argued that religious ideas can influence economic life.
Reason (R): Calvinist values of work and thrift encouraged capitalist accumulation.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; R is Weber's example showing how ideas shape the economy.

qa.q: Schooling is best described as:
qa.a: The formal, institutionalised part of education
qa.e: Schooling has set curricula, teachers and certification.

qa.q: Durkheim believed education's main role is to:
qa.a: Transmit society's shared norms and values
qa.e: Common values bind society together.

qa.q: Why do complex societies need formal schooling?
qa.a: Their knowledge and skills are too specialised to learn from daily life
qa.e: Specialised knowledge requires formal instruction.

qa.q: Universalistic values mean:
qa.a: Applying the same rules to everyone
qa.e: Universalistic norms are impersonal and common.

qa.q: Particularistic values are typical of:
qa.a: The family and kin group
qa.e: Families treat members specially because of relationships.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Education is a lifelong process.
Reason (R): People keep learning through work, media and experience beyond school.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; learning beyond school is why education is lifelong.

qa.q: Case: In a forest community, children learn to fish and identify plants by joining adults daily. This shows:
qa.a: Education through community life in simple societies
qa.e: Learning is embedded in everyday life.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Schools teach only the official syllabus and nothing else.
Reason (R): Schools also transmit shared norms and values.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false; R is true, showing schools teach values beyond the syllabus.

qa.q: According to the functionalist view, education:
qa.a: Prepares people for adult roles and allocates them to jobs
qa.e: Functionalists emphasise preparation and role allocation.

qa.q: According to the conflict view, education:
qa.a: Often reproduces existing social inequalities
qa.e: Unequal schooling passes on advantage and disadvantage.

qa.q: The 'hidden curriculum' refers to:
qa.a: Values and norms taught implicitly in school
qa.e: It includes lessons like obedience and gender roles learned informally.

qa.q: Which is an example of the hidden curriculum?
qa.a: Boys always asked to carry benches and girls to decorate the classroom
qa.e: Such routines teach gender roles without saying so.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Access to education in India is unequal.
Reason (R): Class, caste and gender affect who enrols and who stays in school.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; these factors are the reason access is unequal.

qa.q: Case: Children from a wealthy family attend a school with labs and small classes; children from a slum attend a crowded school with no science teacher. A conflict theorist would say:
qa.a: Education is reproducing class inequality
qa.e: Unequal resources lead to unequal outcomes.

qa.q: The RTE Act reserves what share of entry-level seats in private unaided schools for disadvantaged children?
qa.e: Section 12(1)(c) of the RTE Act, 2009 sets 25%.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Religion and education are both social institutions.
Reason (R): Both are lasting patterns of norms, values and roles meeting social needs.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; R gives the definition that makes both institutions.

qa.q: Which statement is the sociological meaning of culture?
qa.a: The whole learned and shared way of life of a group
qa.e: Sociology uses culture in the broad sense of a way of life.

qa.q: Calling culture a 'map' suggests that culture:
qa.a: Guides people in making sense of the social world
qa.e: Like a map, culture orients behaviour and interpretation.

qa.q: Why can't cultures be ranked as higher or lower?
qa.a: Each culture develops to meet the needs of its setting
qa.e: Cultures are judged by adequacy for their settings.

qa.q: Which is NOT a characteristic of culture?
qa.a: It is inborn and fixed
qa.e: Culture is learned and dynamic, not inherited biologically.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Everyone has culture in the sociological sense.
Reason (R): Sociologically, culture means the entire learned way of life, not only high arts.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; the broad definition is why everyone has culture.

qa.q: The process through which a person learns the culture of a group is:
qa.a: Socialisation
qa.e: Socialisation transmits culture.

qa.q: Case: A villager who has never seen an opera but knows farming rituals, folk songs and local dialects is, sociologically:
qa.a: Fully part of a culture
qa.e: Every way of life is culture.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Culture never changes once it is formed.
Reason (R): Culture is learned and shared by members of a group.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: culture changes. R is true.

qa.q: How did some indigenous Andaman communities survive the 2004 tsunami?
qa.a: By reading natural warning signs through traditional knowledge
qa.e: Traditional ecological knowledge guided them to safety.

qa.q: The tsunami example shows that:
qa.a: Cultures develop knowledge suited to their environments
qa.e: Culture is adapted to settings.

qa.q: A raised finger by a cricket umpire meaning 'out' is an example of:
qa.a: A shared non-verbal code
qa.e: Its meaning is shared by those who know cricket.

qa.q: Non-verbal communication includes:
qa.a: Gestures, facial expressions and signals
qa.e: These carry shared meanings within a culture.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): A gesture can be misunderstood by a person from another culture.
Reason (R): Gestures are learned codes that differ across cultures.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; differences in learned codes cause misunderstanding.

qa.q: Case: A tourist nods to say 'yes', but locals in her host country read it differently. This shows:
qa.a: Non-verbal codes are culturally specific
qa.e: Meaning comes from shared culture.

qa.q: Which communities are named in reports on traditional knowledge during the 2004 tsunami?
qa.a: The Onge and Jarawa of the Andaman Islands
qa.e: The Andaman communities are cited for reading the sea's signs.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Different environments always produce identical cultures.
Reason (R): People develop practices suited to their particular surroundings.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false; R is true and in fact explains why cultures differ.

qa.q: Who defined culture as 'that complex whole which includes knowledge, belief, art, morals, law, custom' and other capabilities?
qa.a: Edward Tylor
qa.e: This is Tylor's 1871 definition.

qa.q: Malinowski's definition of culture is notable for including:
qa.a: Artefacts, goods and technical processes along with ideas and habits
qa.e: He combined material and non-material elements.

qa.q: Malinowski is known as a pioneer of fieldwork in:
qa.a: The Trobriand Islands
qa.e: His Trobriand fieldwork set a model for anthropology.

qa.q: Clifford Geertz described culture as:
qa.a: Webs of meaning through which people interpret experience
qa.e: He saw humans suspended in self-spun webs of significance.

qa.q: Which idea is common to most definitions of culture?
qa.a: It is learned and shared, often through symbols
qa.e: Learning, sharing and symbols run through the definitions.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Malinowski's view of culture covers both material and non-material elements.
Reason (R): His definition lists artefacts and goods as well as ideas, habits and values.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; the list in R is why his view spans both.

qa.q: Case: A researcher studies what tying a rakhi means to siblings rather than listing objects used. She follows the approach of:
qa.a: Clifford Geertz
qa.e: Focusing on meanings reflects Geertz's 'webs of meaning'.

qa.q: Tylor's definition says culture is acquired by humans as:
qa.a: Members of society
qa.e: Culture is acquired through social membership.

qa.q: The three dimensions of culture are:
qa.a: Cognitive, normative and material
qa.e: These are the three dimensions in the chapter.

qa.q: The cognitive dimension of culture refers to:
qa.a: How we learn and make sense of information
qa.e: Cognitive means knowing and understanding.

qa.q: Which is an example of material culture?
qa.a: A mobile phone
qa.e: Material culture includes objects and technology.

qa.q: Culture lag occurs when:
qa.a: Non-material culture changes more slowly than material culture
qa.e: Ogburn described this gap.

qa.q: Who gave the concept of culture lag?
qa.a: W.F. Ogburn
qa.e: Ogburn introduced culture lag.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): In oral cultures, knowledge is kept alive through memory and storytelling.
Reason (R): Oral cultures do not rely on written records.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; without writing, memory and stories carry knowledge.

qa.q: Case: Social media became popular quickly, but norms against spreading fake news developed slowly. This illustrates:
qa.a: Culture lag
qa.e: Technology moved faster than norms.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The three dimensions of culture are completely separate from one another.
Reason (R): A new technology often brings new knowledge and new rules.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false; R is true and shows the dimensions are interrelated.

qa.q: The normative dimension of culture consists of:
qa.a: Folkways, mores, customs, conventions and laws
qa.e: These are rules of conduct.

qa.q: How do norms differ from laws?
qa.a: Norms are implicit; laws are explicit and formally enforced
qa.e: Laws are codified; norms are often unwritten.

qa.q: Which is an example of a law rather than a norm?
qa.a: Wearing a seatbelt in a car
qa.e: It is a written rule enforced by the state.

qa.q: Norms that 'vary by status' means that:
qa.a: Different rules may apply by gender, age or caste
qa.e: Norms can differ by position and can discriminate.

qa.q: Mores differ from folkways because mores:
qa.a: Carry strong moral weight
qa.e: Breaking mores brings strong disapproval.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Some norms can be discriminatory.
Reason (R): Norms often vary according to a person's status, such as gender or caste.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; varying by status is how norms can discriminate.

qa.q: Case: In a village, girls are expected to be home before sunset but boys are not. This is an example of:
qa.a: A norm that varies by gender
qa.e: An unwritten rule applied differently by status.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Laws are implicit, unwritten rules.
Reason (R): Laws are formally enforced by the state.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: laws are explicit and written. R is true.

qa.q: Sociologically, identity is formed through:
qa.a: The roles we play and the groups we belong to
qa.e: Identity is a social product.

qa.q: A sub-culture is:
qa.a: A group within a larger culture with distinct styles and values
qa.e: 'Sub' means within, not lower.

qa.q: Which is an example of a sub-culture?
qa.a: Skateboarders with their own slang and dress
qa.e: They share distinctive styles within the wider culture.

qa.q: Shared codes linked to roles mean that:
qa.a: People in related roles understand each other's expected behaviour
qa.e: Role-players share understandings of how to act.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Belonging to a sub-culture can shape a teenager's identity.
Reason (R): Sub-cultures give members a sense of belonging and difference.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; belonging and difference are how sub-cultures shape identity.

qa.q: Case: Ravi is captain at school, a younger brother at home and a trainee at a music class. This shows that:
qa.a: Identity is formed through multiple roles
qa.e: Each role contributes to his identity.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The word 'sub-culture' implies that the group's culture is inferior.
Reason (R): A sub-culture is a distinct group within a larger culture.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: 'sub' means within, not lower. R is true.

qa.q: Which statement about identity and culture is correct?
qa.a: Identity draws on shared cultural codes and group membership
qa.e: Identity is formed within culture.

qa.q: Ethnocentrism means:
qa.a: Judging other cultures by one's own culture's standards
qa.e: It assumes one's own culture is the yardstick.

qa.q: Macaulay's Minute on Indian Education was issued in:
qa.e: It dates to 1835 and favoured English education.

qa.q: Macaulay's Minute is an example of:
qa.a: Colonial ethnocentrism
qa.e: It dismissed Indian knowledge as inferior.

qa.q: Cosmopolitanism is best described as:
qa.a: Valuing other cultures and borrowing from them openly
qa.e: It welcomes cultural exchange.

qa.q: The English words 'bungalow' and 'pyjama' illustrate:
qa.a: Cultural borrowing
qa.e: English absorbed words from Indian languages.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Cosmopolitanism suits modern societies.
Reason (R): Migration, media and trade bring constant contact between cultures.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; constant contact makes openness to other cultures valuable.

qa.q: Case: A school celebrates Onam, Bihu, Eid, Christmas and Lohri, with students learning about each. This reflects:
qa.a: Cosmopolitanism
qa.e: Valuing and learning from many cultures.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Ethnocentrism usually arises when cultures come into contact.
Reason (R): People then compare others to their own culture's standards.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; contact prompts comparison, which can become ethnocentric.

qa.q: Which is an internal cause of cultural change?
qa.a: A new invention made within the society
qa.e: Internal causes arise within the society.

qa.q: Which is an external cause of cultural change?
qa.a: Contact with another culture through trade
qa.e: External causes come from outside.

qa.q: Revolutionary change is:
qa.a: Rapid and sweeping
qa.e: Revolutions transform society quickly.

qa.q: Which is a classic example of revolutionary change?
qa.a: The French Revolution
qa.e: It rapidly overturned monarchy and old order.

qa.q: In which year did the French Revolution, the classic example of revolutionary cultural change, begin?
qa.e: It began in 1789.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Ecological change can cause cultural change.
Reason (R): When forests or rivers are destroyed, communities must alter their ways of life.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; R describes how ecological change forces cultural change.

qa.q: Case: Over 50 years, more women in a town took up paid jobs and family routines slowly changed. This is:
qa.a: Evolutionary change
qa.e: Slow and gradual change is evolutionary.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): All cultural change is slow and gradual.
Reason (R): Revolutions can transform a culture in a few years.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false; R is true and gives the counter-example.

qa.q: Socialisation is best defined as:
qa.a: The lifelong process by which an infant becomes a self-aware person
qa.e: It is how we learn culture and become social.

qa.q: Primary socialisation takes place mainly in:
qa.a: The family during early childhood
qa.e: The family is the main agency in early childhood.

qa.q: Which is an example of re-socialisation?
qa.a: A new army recruit learning military discipline
qa.e: Re-socialisation involves unlearning and relearning in a new setting.

qa.q: Cases of feral or isolated children show that:
qa.a: Social contact is necessary for normal human development
qa.e: Without interaction children do not develop language and social skills.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Socialisation is not mere programming.
Reason (R): Individuals actively interpret and sometimes resist what they learn.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; active interpretation is why socialisation is not programming.

qa.q: Secondary socialisation occurs through:
qa.a: School, peer groups, work and wider society
qa.e: It follows primary socialisation.

qa.q: Case: An Indian student who moves to Japan learns to bow, remove shoes at work and follow strict punctuality. This is:
qa.a: Re-socialisation
qa.e: She unlearns some norms and learns new ones.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Socialisation is a lifelong process.
Reason (R): Socialisation ends when a person becomes an adult.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: A is true. R is false: socialisation continues through work, re-socialisation and new roles.

qa.q: Which is usually the first agency of socialisation?
qa.a: The family
qa.e: Primary socialisation happens mainly in the family.

qa.q: Peer groups differ from family in that peer relations are:
qa.a: Based more on equality among people of similar age
qa.e: Peers relate as equals.

qa.q: In the context of school as an agency of socialisation, the hidden curriculum means:
qa.a: Lessons learned implicitly in school, such as obedience or gender roles
qa.e: It is taught through routines and expectations.

qa.q: Socialisation in the family varies according to:
qa.a: Family system, region and class
qa.e: Different families pass on different norms.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Peer pressure can strongly influence teenagers.
Reason (R): Peer groups are important agencies of socialisation for young people.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; because peers socialise teens, their pressure matters.

qa.q: Case: In a school, girls are always asked to welcome guests with flowers and boys to arrange chairs. This illustrates:
qa.a: The hidden curriculum of gender roles
qa.e: Routines teach gendered expectations without stating them.

qa.q: Which of these is mainly learned through peers?
qa.a: Slang and fashion trends of one's age group
qa.e: Age-group norms often come from peers.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Schools teach only academic subjects.
Reason (R): Schools also teach values like punctuality and obedience.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false; R is true and shows schools teach more than subjects.

qa.q: Which of these is an agency of socialisation?
qa.a: Mass media
qa.e: Media spreads norms, values and role models.

qa.q: Gendered socialisation means:
qa.a: Boys and girls are raised with different expectations
qa.e: Different toys, chores and freedoms teach gender roles.

qa.q: Krishna Kumar's 'Growing up Male' is concerned with:
qa.a: How boys are socialised into masculine roles
qa.e: It discusses masculine socialisation.

qa.q: Which is an example of agencies of socialisation conflicting?
qa.a: School teaching equality while family enforces unequal roles
qa.e: Different agencies send different messages.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Socialisation can produce individuality and independent thinking.
Reason (R): Through socialisation we acquire language and ideas that let us reflect on and question norms.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; acquiring tools of thought is how socialisation enables individuality.

qa.q: Which is NOT listed among 'other agencies' of socialisation?
qa.a: Ocean tides
qa.e: Tides are natural, not social agencies.

qa.q: Case: A teenage boy is told 'boys don't cry' at home, but a TV show praises emotional honesty in men. This shows:
qa.a: Conflict between agencies of socialisation
qa.e: Family and media send opposite messages.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Mass media is an important modern agency of socialisation.
Reason (R): Sociologists agree that mass media completely determines people's attitudes.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: A is true. R is false: there is debate about how far media shapes or merely reflects attitudes.

qa.q: In Giddens' clock analogy, modern societies appear at about:
qa.e: Modern societies emerge only in the last 30 seconds of the 24-hour day.

qa.q: The clock analogy is used to show that:
qa.a: Rapid continuous social change is recent in human history
qa.e: It highlights how little time modern societies occupy.

qa.q: Social change refers to change that is:
qa.a: Intensive and extensive
qa.e: It deeply affects society and affects many people.

qa.q: 'Extensive' change means change that:
qa.a: Affects a large part of society
qa.e: Extensive refers to breadth of impact.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Social change must be studied alongside social order.
Reason (R): Social order includes forces that resist and regulate change.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; because order resists change, both must be studied together.

qa.q: Which is the best example of social change?
qa.a: The spread of universal schooling over decades
qa.e: It deeply and widely changed society.

qa.q: Case: Your grandmother never used a bank; your mother uses one; you pay by UPI. This sequence best illustrates:
qa.a: Rapid social change within a few generations
qa.e: Major changes in economic life across three generations.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Rapid social change has been a feature of all of human history.
Reason (R): Agriculture and civilisations appear only near the end of Giddens' 24-hour day.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false; R is true and shows change accelerated only recently.

qa.q: Evolutionary change in society is:
qa.a: Slow and gradual
qa.e: The term comes from Darwin's gradual evolution.

qa.q: Social Darwinism was used to:
qa.a: Justify the dominance of some groups as 'the fittest'
qa.e: It applied 'survival of the fittest' to societies to justify inequality.

qa.q: The shift from metal coins to paper money is an example of:
qa.a: Structural change
qa.e: It changed how economic exchange is structured.

qa.q: Changing ideas about childhood that made child labour unacceptable are an example of:
qa.a: Change in ideas and values
qa.e: The change is in how society values childhood.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The word 'revolution' is also used for changes outside politics.
Reason (R): Terms like the Industrial Revolution and Green Revolution describe rapid changes in production.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; these examples show the wider use of the term.

qa.q: Why is social change hard to define?
qa.a: Almost everything changes, so sociologists must focus on significant change
qa.e: The concept needs limits to be useful.

qa.q: Case: Within a few years, a country's monarchy is overthrown and a republic is declared. This is:
qa.a: Revolutionary change
qa.e: Rapid political transformation is revolutionary.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Social Darwinism is accepted by sociologists today as a valid explanation of inequality.
Reason (R): Social Darwinism claimed powerful groups dominated because they were 'fittest'.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: it is rejected. R is true as a description of what it claimed.

qa.q: Which is an environmental cause of social change?
qa.a: A tsunami destroying coastal villages
qa.e: Natural disasters are environmental causes.

qa.q: The discovery of oil in West Asia is an example of how:
qa.a: A newly found natural resource can transform society
qa.e: Oil wealth transformed economies and societies.

qa.q: Which is a technological cause of social change?
qa.a: Steam power
qa.e: Steam power transformed industry and transport.

qa.q: The World Trade Organization (WTO) is linked to social change through:
qa.a: Global trade rules that affect industries and farmers
qa.e: Trade rules shape markets and livelihoods.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Technology often changes society in ways nobody planned.
Reason (R): New technologies alter work, travel and social relations beyond their original purpose.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; the wide effects of technology explain its unplanned impact.

qa.q: Case: A river changes course and a riverside village loses its farmland; families migrate to towns for work. The cause of change is:
qa.a: Environmental
qa.e: A natural change forced migration.

qa.q: Different ways of life in desert, cold-mountain and river-valley societies show the influence of:
qa.a: Environment
qa.e: Geography and climate shape culture and livelihood.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Plantation economies moved large numbers of workers across continents.
Reason (R): Plantations needed large supplies of labour.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; the demand for labour is why workers were moved.

qa.q: Which is a political cause of social change?
qa.a: Introduction of universal adult franchise
qa.e: Voting rights reshape power relations.

qa.q: Universal adult franchise means:
qa.a: Every adult citizen has the right to vote
qa.e: It gives equal votes regardless of caste, class or gender.

qa.q: Weber's 'Protestant ethic' argument is an example of:
qa.a: A cultural (religious) cause of change
qa.e: Religious ideas encouraged capitalist behaviour.

qa.q: The Bhakti movement is cited as a cultural cause of change because it:
qa.a: Questioned caste hierarchy and ritualism through religious ideas
qa.e: Religious ideas challenged social hierarchy.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Cricket can be seen as part of cultural change in India.
Reason (R): Cricket spread from a colonial elite game to a mass passion across classes.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; its spread across classes is the cultural change.

qa.q: Changes in the status of women (education, work, property) are best classified as:
qa.a: A cultural cause of change
qa.e: Changing ideas about women's roles transformed society.

qa.q: Case: After a country becomes independent, it abolishes titles of nobility and gives equal votes to all. The main cause of change here is:
qa.a: Political
qa.e: State and political decisions drive this change.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Political changes never affect people's ideas and values.
Reason (R): Universal adult franchise gave equal political rights to all adults.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: political changes like franchise reshape ideas of equality. R is true.

qa.q: Social order refers to:
qa.a: Patterns of behaviour that persist and resist change
qa.e: Order is the stability that regulates change.

qa.q: Which groups tend to favour stability?
qa.a: Dominant groups who benefit from existing arrangements
qa.e: Those who gain from the status quo resist change.

qa.q: Spontaneous consent means order is maintained through:
qa.a: Shared values and norms learned through socialisation
qa.e: People follow rules because they believe in them.

qa.q: Coercion means maintaining order through:
qa.a: Force, law and punishment
qa.e: Coercion uses power to compel compliance.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Subordinate groups are more likely to seek social change.
Reason (R): They gain less from existing arrangements.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; having less to lose and more to gain is why they seek change.

qa.q: Case: A family follows its traditional festival customs because all members value them. Order here is maintained mainly by:
qa.a: Spontaneous consent
qa.e: Shared values produce willing compliance.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Most societies maintain order through a mix of consent and coercion.
Reason (R): Shared values alone or force alone rarely keep order fully.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; since neither works alone, societies combine them.

qa.q: Why would life be very difficult if social rules changed every day?
qa.a: People could not predict others' behaviour or plan ahead
qa.e: Order makes cooperation and planning possible.

qa.q: Domination refers to:
qa.a: Power exercised in a stable, routine way
qa.e: Domination is routinised power.

qa.q: Legitimacy means:
qa.a: Acceptance of power as just and proper
qa.e: Legitimate power is seen as rightful.

qa.q: According to Weber, authority is:
qa.a: Legitimate power
qa.e: Authority is power accepted as legitimate.

qa.q: Law is best defined as:
qa.a: An explicit, codified norm enforced by the state
qa.e: Laws are written and state-enforced.

qa.q: Which is an example of informal authority?
qa.a: A religious sect leader obeyed by followers
qa.e: Authority accepted without formal legal office.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): A police officer's orders are usually obeyed.
Reason (R): The police officer's power is backed by law and accepted as legitimate.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; legitimacy and legal backing explain obedience.

qa.q: Case: In a village, everyone accepts the decision of a respected elder in a family dispute, though he holds no official post. His position is:
qa.a: Informal authority
qa.e: People accept his power as legitimate without law.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): A thief who forces a victim to hand over money exercises authority.
Reason (R): The thief's power is not accepted as legitimate.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false; R is true and is the reason it is not authority.

qa.q: Contestation means:
qa.a: Dissent and disagreement with the established order
qa.e: It covers forms of challenging existing arrangements.

qa.q: Crime is best defined as:
qa.a: An act that breaks a law
qa.e: Crime is defined by law, not by morality.

qa.q: Gandhi's Salt Satyagraha is an example of:
qa.a: Deliberately breaking an unjust law as protest
qa.e: Civil disobedience against the salt law.

qa.q: The Salt Satyagraha took place in:
qa.e: The Dandi march was in 1930.

qa.q: Weber argued that the modern state claims:
qa.a: A monopoly over the legitimate use of violence
qa.e: Only the state's force is treated as legitimate.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Elections can be seen as institutionalised contestation.
Reason (R): In elections, groups peacefully compete for power under agreed rules.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; peaceful competition under rules is what institutionalises contestation.

qa.q: A counter-culture is:
qa.a: A group that rejects some dominant values of society
qa.e: Counter-cultures express contestation.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Crime is an act that breaks a law.
Reason (R): All crimes are acts of violence.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: A is true. R is false: many crimes, such as tax evasion, involve no violence.

qa.q: Villages emerged mainly because of:
qa.a: Settled agriculture producing a surplus
qa.e: Settled farming allowed permanent settlements.

qa.q: The rural-urban distinction is based mainly on:
qa.a: Population density and the share of agricultural work
qa.e: Urban areas are denser and less agricultural.

qa.q: What is the minimum population for a census town in India?
qa.e: A census town needs at least 5,000 people.

qa.q: For a census town, at least what percentage of the male main working population must be in non-agricultural work?
qa.e: The Census uses the 75% criterion.

qa.q: What is the minimum population density for a census town?
qa.a: 400 persons per sq km
qa.e: Density must be at least 400 per sq km.

qa.q: A settlement has 7,000 people, 70% of male main workers in non-farm jobs and density 500 per sq km. Why is it NOT a census town?
qa.a: It fails the 75% non-agricultural workers test
qa.e: 70% is below 75%; the other two tests are met.

qa.q: In the Census of India, an 'urban agglomeration' refers to:
qa.a: A town with its outgrowths, or two or more contiguous towns, forming one urban spread
qa.e: An urban agglomeration is a continuous urban spread formed by a town and its adjoining outgrowths, or by two or more physically contiguous towns.

qa.q: About what share of India's population was urban in the 2011 Census?
qa.a: About 31%
qa.e: The 2011 Census recorded roughly 31% urban population.

qa.q: Social order is generally stronger in villages because:
qa.a: They are small and face-to-face, with little anonymity
qa.e: Close ties and dependence make deviation visible and costly.

qa.q: The concept of 'dominant caste' was developed by:
qa.a: M.N. Srinivas
qa.e: Srinivas described landowning, numerically strong, powerful castes.

qa.q: Which is NOT a feature of a dominant caste as described by Srinivas?
qa.a: Being the smallest group with no land
qa.e: Dominance rests on numbers, land and power.

qa.q: Land reforms in India included:
qa.a: Abolition of zamindari, tenancy reforms and land ceilings
qa.e: These aimed to redistribute land and protect tenants.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Land reforms aimed to change rural power relations.
Reason (R): Control over land was the basis of landlord power in villages.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; since land meant power, redistributing land targeted power.

qa.q: Case: In a village, one caste owns 70% of the land, is the largest group and controls the panchayat. Sociologically it is a:
qa.a: Dominant caste
qa.e: Numbers, land and political power define dominance.

qa.q: Operation Barga, a land reform programme, was carried out in:
qa.a: West Bengal
qa.e: It recorded sharecroppers' rights in West Bengal.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Land reforms were equally successful across all Indian states.
Reason (R): Some states, like Kerala and West Bengal, implemented them more effectively.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false; R is true and shows the variation.

qa.q: MGNREGA guarantees how many days of wage employment per rural household per year?
qa.e: The Act guarantees up to 100 days per household per year.

qa.q: The Green Revolution involved:
qa.a: High-yielding seeds, irrigation and fertilisers
qa.e: These technologies raised crop yields.

qa.q: A common effect of agricultural technology on labour relations was:
qa.a: A shift from payment in kind to cash wages
qa.e: Commercial farming spread cash wages and casual hiring.

qa.q: MGNREGA was enacted in:
qa.e: The Act was passed in 2005.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Rural employment schemes can raise labourers' bargaining power.
Reason (R): Guaranteed work provides an alternative to depending on a single landowner.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; having an alternative is why bargaining power rises.

qa.q: Which is a problem often reported in rural employment schemes?
qa.a: Delayed wage payments
qa.e: Delays and leakages are commonly reported.

qa.q: Case: In a Punjab village after the Green Revolution, landowners hire migrant labourers for harvest and pay daily cash wages. This shows:
qa.a: Casual, cash-based labour replacing attached labour
qa.e: Commercial farming changed labour relations.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Technological change in agriculture had only economic effects.
Reason (R): New seeds and machines also changed labour relations and village power.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false; R is true and shows the social effects.

qa.q: Urbanism as a way of life is marked by:
qa.a: Anonymity, individualism and impersonal relations
qa.e: Large, dense, diverse cities produce anonymity.

qa.q: The idea of 'urbanism as a way of life' is associated with:
qa.a: Louis Wirth
qa.e: Wirth described the urban way of life.

qa.q: Why is space central to understanding cities?
qa.a: Where people live reflects divisions of class, caste, religion and ethnicity
qa.e: Residential patterns reveal social divisions.

qa.q: A slum is best described as:
qa.a: A dense area with poor housing and inadequate basic services
qa.e: Slums lack adequate water, sanitation and housing.

qa.q: Ghettoisation refers to:
qa.a: Concentration of a particular community in one area, often for security
qa.e: Communities cluster, often due to discrimination or fear.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Cities can offer migrants freedom from traditional social controls.
Reason (R): Urban anonymity weakens the face-to-face control of family and community.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; anonymity is the reason for the freedom.

qa.q: Case: After riots in a city, families of one community sell their homes in mixed areas and move to a neighbourhood where their community is in a majority. This is:
qa.a: Ghettoisation
qa.e: Clustering for security after conflict is ghettoisation.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Many slum residents provide essential labour to the city and run small industries.
Reason (R): Slums have adequate housing and basic services.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: A is true. R is false: slums are marked by poor housing and inadequate services.

qa.q: A gated community is:
qa.a: An enclosed affluent enclave with private security and services
qa.e: Walls, guards and private services mark gated communities.

qa.q: Gentrification refers to:
qa.a: Upgrading poorer neighbourhoods, often displacing earlier residents
qa.e: Rising costs push out original residents.

qa.q: Who usually loses in gentrification?
qa.a: Poorer original residents who are priced out
qa.e: Displacement hits the poor most.

qa.q: Which statement about urban transport is correct?
qa.a: Long commutes by crowded trains, buses and metros are common
qa.e: Commuting shapes daily life and housing choices.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Gated communities can deepen spatial segregation in cities.
Reason (R): They wall off affluent residents and their services from the rest of the city.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; walling off is how they deepen segregation.

qa.q: Which feature is more typical of rural than urban social order?
qa.a: Face-to-face control and dependence on dominant groups
qa.e: Villages have closer ties and dependence.

qa.q: Case: Rents in an old Delhi neighbourhood rise after cafés and boutiques open, and long-time tenants move to the city's edge. This is:
qa.a: Gentrification
qa.e: Upgrading and displacement define gentrification.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Gated communities rely only on public services provided by the city.
Reason (R): Gated communities typically arrange private security, water and power backup.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false; R is true and contradicts A.

qa.q: Sociology emerged as a product of:
qa.a: The age of revolutions in Western Europe
qa.e: The Enlightenment, French and Industrial Revolutions shaped it.

qa.q: Which set of ideas did the Enlightenment promote?
qa.a: Reason, secular and scientific thinking
qa.e: It promoted rational, secular and humanistic thought.

qa.q: The ideals of the French Revolution were:
qa.a: Liberty, equality and fraternity
qa.e: These became the slogans of modern democracy.

qa.q: The French Revolution began in:
qa.e: It began in 1789.

qa.q: One effect of the French Revolution was the separation of:
qa.a: The public sphere of the state from the private sphere of home and religion
qa.e: It defined the modern citizen in the public sphere.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The age of revolutions encouraged the rise of sociology.
Reason (R): These revolutions showed that society could be changed by human action and therefore studied rationally.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; seeing society as human-made made a science of it possible.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The French Revolution strengthened the Church's control over the state.
Reason (R): The Revolution ended feudal privileges.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: it reduced the Church's dominance. R is true.

qa.q: Case: A student argues that because humans created the social order, humans can study and reform it. This idea draws most directly on:
qa.a: Enlightenment thinking
qa.e: Reason applied to human affairs is an Enlightenment idea.

qa.q: The Industrial Revolution is best described as:
qa.a: The application of science and technology to production
qa.e: It transformed production with machines and new energy sources.

qa.q: Which was a social effect of industrialisation in Europe?
qa.a: Growth of urban slums and poverty
qa.e: Rapid urban growth created slums.

qa.q: Why did states take on new roles in the 19th century?
qa.a: To deal with urban health and sanitation
qa.e: New urban problems demanded public action.

qa.q: Sociology was seen as the 'science of the new industrial society' because:
qa.a: It arose to understand changes brought by industrialisation
qa.e: It responded to the need to understand industrial society.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Industrialisation created a need for systematic knowledge about society.
Reason (R): States had to plan for health, housing and sanitation in growing cities.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; state planning needs are why systematic knowledge was needed.

qa.q: Case: A 19th-century city faces cholera in crowded workers' districts, and officials start counting households and sanitation. This reflects:
qa.a: The state's new responsibility and need for social knowledge
qa.e: Public health work required data.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The Industrial Revolution affected only the economy, not social life.
Reason (R): It drew people to cities and transformed living conditions.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false; R is true and shows the social effects.

qa.q: Which revolution is most directly linked with factories, slums and new labour organisation?
qa.a: The Industrial Revolution
qa.e: Factories and slums were industrial outcomes.

qa.q: The Communist Manifesto (1848) was written by:
qa.a: Marx and Engels
qa.e: Marx co-authored it with Friedrich Engels.

qa.q: Marx was born in:
qa.e: He was born in 1818 and died in 1883.

qa.q: Marx called his approach:
qa.a: Scientific socialism
qa.e: He believed scientific analysis showed how capitalism could be replaced.

qa.q: For Marx, the base of society is:
qa.a: Its economic structure
qa.e: The economic structure is the foundation.

qa.q: Which belongs to the superstructure?
qa.a: Law and politics
qa.e: Ideas, law, politics, religion form the superstructure.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Marx believed that economic structure shapes ideas and laws.
Reason (R): For Marx, the base is the foundation on which the superstructure rests.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; R states the base-superstructure model that explains A.

qa.q: Marx's major work analysing capitalism is:
qa.a: Capital
qa.e: Capital (first volume 1867) analyses capitalism.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Marx saw capitalism as a fully just system that should last forever.
Reason (R): Marx aimed to end exploitation and oppression.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: he criticised capitalism and expected its replacement. R is true.

qa.q: Which is an example of a means of production?
qa.a: Machinery
qa.e: Tools and machines are means of production.

qa.q: Relations of production refer to:
qa.a: Economic relationships, especially ownership, in production
qa.e: They define who owns and who works.

qa.q: The mode of production is:
qa.a: The combination of means and relations of production
qa.e: Together they characterise a type of society.

qa.q: Which is the correct sequence of Marx's stages?
qa.a: Primitive communism, slavery, feudalism, capitalism
qa.e: This is Marx's historical sequence, with socialism expected next.

qa.q: The two main classes of feudalism, in Marx's view, were:
qa.a: Lords and serfs
qa.e: Feudal production rested on lords and serfs.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Primitive communism had no class division.
Reason (R): Means of production were held in common.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; common ownership is why there were no classes.

qa.q: Case: In ancient Rome, a landowner owns both the land and the workers, who can be bought and sold like property. This is the mode of production Marx called:
qa.a: Slavery
qa.e: Ownership of human beings as property marks the slave mode of production of the ancient world.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Marx predicted a transition from capitalism to socialism.
Reason (R): Marx believed capitalism would be the final stage of history.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: A is true. R is false and contradicts A: Marx expected capitalism to be overthrown.

qa.q: For Marx, a class is defined by:
qa.a: Its position in the production process
qa.e: Ownership or non-ownership of the means of production defines class.

qa.q: The bourgeoisie are:
qa.a: Owners of the means of production
qa.e: Capitalists own factories, machines and capital.

qa.q: The proletariat (working class) owns:
qa.a: Only its capacity to work
qa.e: Workers must sell labour power to survive.

qa.q: Alienation, in Marx's sense, refers to workers being:
qa.a: Estranged from their products, work process, fellow workers and themselves
qa.e: Capitalist production separates workers from control and meaning.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Capitalists and workers have opposed interests.
Reason (R): Capitalists seek profit, partly by keeping wage costs low, while workers seek higher wages.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; the clash over wages and profit is why interests are opposed.

qa.q: Case: A factory worker assembles one tiny part all day, has no say in the design and never sees the finished phone. This best illustrates:
qa.a: Alienation
qa.e: Lack of control over product and process is alienation.

qa.q: Under capitalism, workers must sell their labour because:
qa.a: They do not own the means of production
qa.e: Without means of production, labour is all they have to sell.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Members of the same class share common interests.
Reason (R): They occupy the same position in the production process.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; shared position creates shared interests.

qa.q: For Marx, the driving force of history is:
qa.a: Class struggle
qa.e: Conflict between classes moves history forward.

qa.q: Class consciousness means:
qa.a: Awareness among a class of its shared interests
qa.e: It is awareness of common class interests and opposition.

qa.q: According to Marx, class consciousness develops through:
qa.a: Political mobilisation and organisation
qa.e: Shared position must be turned into awareness through mobilisation.

qa.q: For Marx, a revolution is:
qa.a: The overthrow of a ruling class by an oppressed class
qa.e: It brings a new mode of production.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Workers who share the same economic position may still not act together.
Reason (R): Class consciousness has to develop through political mobilisation.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; the need for mobilisation explains why shared position is not enough.

qa.q: The line 'The history of all hitherto existing society is the history of class struggles' is from:
qa.a: The Communist Manifesto
qa.e: It opens the first section of the Manifesto.

qa.q: Case: Tea-garden workers from different language groups form one union and strike for higher wages. In Marx's terms this shows:
qa.a: Class consciousness leading to class struggle
qa.e: Unity across divisions reflects class consciousness.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): For Marx, ideas are the main cause of historical change, not economic structure.
Reason (R): Marx held that the economic base shapes the superstructure.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false for Marx; R is true and contradicts A.

qa.q: Durkheim is regarded as a founder of sociology as:
qa.a: A formal academic discipline
qa.e: He established sociology's distinct subject matter and methods.

qa.q: Which is Durkheim's work?
qa.a: The Rules of Sociological Method
qa.e: Rules (1895) sets out his method.

qa.q: Durkheim's study 'Suicide' was published in:
qa.e: Suicide appeared in 1897.

qa.q: Social facts are:
qa.a: Ways of acting and thinking external to individuals that constrain them
qa.e: They are collective and constraining.

qa.q: Durkheim argued that social facts should be studied:
qa.a: Scientifically, 'as things'
qa.e: He stressed an objective, scientific approach.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Language is an example of a social fact.
Reason (R): Language exists outside individuals and constrains how they communicate.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; externality and constraint make language a social fact.

qa.q: Case: A researcher finds that suicide rates are lower among people with strong family and community ties. Following Durkheim, this shows that:
qa.a: Suicide rates are social facts linked to social integration
qa.e: Rates vary with social bonds.

qa.q: Durkheim founded the journal:
qa.a: L'Année Sociologique
qa.e: He founded L'Année Sociologique.

qa.q: Mechanical solidarity is based on:
qa.a: Likeness and a strong collective conscience
qa.e: Similar people sharing beliefs form mechanical solidarity.

qa.q: Organic solidarity is based on:
qa.a: Difference and interdependence from the division of labour
qa.e: Specialisation makes people depend on each other.

qa.q: The type of law associated with mechanical solidarity is:
qa.a: Repressive
qa.e: It punishes to express collective outrage.

qa.q: Restitutive law aims to:
qa.a: Restore things to how they were, e.g. through compensation
qa.e: It repairs harm rather than punishing.

qa.q: Why did Durkheim study law to understand solidarity?
qa.a: Solidarity is not directly observable, but law is
qa.e: Law makes the invisible moral bond visible.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Large modern societies tend to have restitutive law.
Reason (R): They are held together by organic solidarity based on interdependence.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; organic solidarity's need to repair relations explains restitutive law.

qa.q: Case: In a small community, a person who breaks a taboo is publicly punished to show the group's anger. This indicates:
qa.a: Mechanical solidarity
qa.e: Repressive punishment reflects strong collective conscience.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Organic solidarity is found mainly in large, modern societies.
Reason (R): Organic solidarity rests on likeness and a strong collective conscience.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: A is true. R is false: that describes mechanical solidarity; organic solidarity rests on difference and interdependence.

qa.q: Durkheim used the division of labour to explain:
qa.a: The shift from simple to modern societies
qa.e: Specialisation marks the transition to modern society.

qa.q: According to Durkheim, increasing population density leads to:
qa.a: Greater division of labour
qa.e: More interaction and competition encourage specialisation.

qa.q: In modern societies, the collective conscience:
qa.a: Weakens and becomes more general
qa.e: Difference among individuals weakens shared beliefs.

qa.q: Voluntary associations are groups that people:
qa.a: Join by choice
qa.e: Modern individuals choose their associations.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Modern society gives individuals more autonomy.
Reason (R): Specialisation and a weaker collective conscience leave more room for individual choice.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; R explains why autonomy grows.

qa.q: Durkheim's book on this theme is:
qa.a: The Division of Labour in Society
qa.e: Published in 1893.

qa.q: Case: A young person from a small town moves to a city, chooses a new career, joins a cycling club and an environmental NGO. Durkheim would see this as:
qa.a: Individual autonomy and voluntary association in modern society
qa.e: Choice of occupation and associations marks modern autonomy.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): In Durkheim's view, specialisation makes people more alike.
Reason (R): Specialisation means people do different tasks.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: specialisation makes people more different. R is true.

qa.q: Weber's interpretive sociology focuses on:
qa.a: The subjective meanings of social action
qa.e: Understanding meanings is central to Weber.

qa.q: Weber argued that social sciences need different methods from natural sciences because:
qa.a: Human action is guided by meanings
qa.e: Meanings must be interpreted, not just measured.

qa.q: Empathetic understanding (Verstehen) means:
qa.a: Putting oneself in the actor's place to grasp meanings
qa.e: It is a method of understanding, not sympathy.

qa.q: Value neutrality requires a sociologist to:
qa.a: Describe others' values objectively without judging them
qa.e: Researchers should not let their own values distort description.

qa.q: Weber lived from:
qa.e: Weber's dates are 1864–1920.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Weber emphasised understanding the meanings behind social action.
Reason (R): Weber believed humans act on the basis of meanings they attach to situations.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; because action depends on meaning, meanings must be understood.

qa.q: Case: A sociologist studying a festival says, 'Their ritual is foolish superstition.' Which Weberian principle is violated?
qa.a: Value neutrality
qa.e: Judging others' beliefs breaks value neutrality.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Weber believed sociology should copy the natural sciences exactly.
Reason (R): Weber stressed the role of subjective meaning in human action.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false; R is true and is why he rejected a copy of natural science.

qa.q: An ideal type is:
qa.a: A logical model highlighting key features, used for analysis
qa.e: It is an analytical tool, not a description or ideal.

qa.q: Traditional authority is based on:
qa.a: Custom and long-established practice
qa.e: Kings and hereditary chiefs are examples.

qa.q: Charismatic authority is based on:
qa.a: Extraordinary personal qualities attributed to a leader
qa.e: Followers believe in the leader's special qualities.

qa.q: Rational-legal authority is based on:
qa.a: Impersonal rules and legal procedures
qa.e: Obedience is owed to the office defined by law.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): A transferred officer loses authority in the old post.
Reason (R): In rational-legal authority, power belongs to the office, not the person.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; authority tied to office is why it is lost on transfer.

qa.q: Case: Followers of a spiritual leader obey him because they believe he has divine gifts, though he holds no office. His authority is:
qa.a: Charismatic
qa.e: Authority from perceived extraordinary qualities is charismatic.

qa.q: Why did Weber use ideal types?
qa.a: To compare and analyse real cases against a clear model
qa.e: Ideal types are measuring sticks.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Weber's ideal type of authority describes perfectly what every leader is like.
Reason (R): Ideal types exaggerate key features and real cases often mix them.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false; R is true and contradicts A.

qa.q: Bureaucracy is the typical organisation of:
qa.a: Rational-legal authority
qa.e: Rules and offices define bureaucracy.

qa.q: Which is a feature of Weber's bureaucracy?
qa.a: Reliance on written documents
qa.e: Files and records are central.

qa.q: 'Fixed area of jurisdiction' means that:
qa.a: Each office has defined duties and powers set by rules
qa.e: Rules define the scope of each office.

qa.q: Hierarchical ordering of positions refers to:
qa.a: A chain of command with higher offices supervising lower ones
qa.e: Hierarchy ensures supervision and control.

qa.q: Separation of public office from private life means:
qa.a: The official cannot use the office for private benefit
qa.e: Office resources and powers belong to the organisation.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Bureaucracies employ trained, specialised staff.
Reason (R): Office management requires expert knowledge and specialised skills.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; the need for expertise explains the training.

qa.q: Case: A government clerk takes cash from applicants to speed up their files and keeps it. Which feature of bureaucracy is violated?
qa.a: Separation of office from private life
qa.e: Using office for private gain breaks this principle.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Weber saw bureaucracy as based on impersonal rules.
Reason (R): In a bureaucracy, officials may use their office for private benefit.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: A is true. R is false: bureaucracy separates the office from the official's private life.

qa.q: Sociology was first taught in India at the University of:
qa.a: Bombay
qa.e: Bombay began teaching sociology in 1919.

qa.q: In which year did sociology begin to be taught at Bombay?
qa.e: Teaching began in 1919.

qa.q: Which universities started sociology programmes in the 1920s, after Bombay?
qa.a: Calcutta and Lucknow
qa.e: Calcutta and Lucknow followed in the 1920s.

qa.q: A key question for early Indian sociologists was:
qa.a: Whether Western social anthropology fitted Indians studying India
qa.e: They questioned the fit of Western disciplines.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): We should study India's founding sociologists critically.
Reason (R): Critical study allows later generations to build on and revise their ideas.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; building on their work requires critical engagement.

qa.q: 'Indianising' sociology meant:
qa.a: Adapting the discipline to Indian social realities
qa.e: Founders developed approaches suited to India.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Sociology was first taught in India at the University of Bombay in 1919.
Reason (R): Sociology began to be taught in India only after Independence.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: A is true. R is false: teaching began in 1919, under colonial rule.

qa.q: Case: A student says, 'Ghurye said it, so it must be true for ever.' What would the chapter suggest?
qa.a: Study founders critically so their ideas can be built upon
qa.e: The chapter encourages critical engagement.

qa.q: L.K. Ananthakrishna Iyer began his career as a:
qa.a: Clerk
qa.e: He was a clerk, then a teacher, before becoming an ethnographer.

qa.q: Ananthakrishna Iyer is associated with ethnographic work in:
qa.a: Cochin
qa.e: He studied Cochin State.

qa.q: Sarat Chandra Roy studied which tribal communities?
qa.a: The Oraon, Munda and Kharia
qa.e: These communities lived around Ranchi.

qa.q: The journal 'Man in India' was founded by:
qa.a: Sarat Chandra Roy
qa.e: S.C. Roy founded Man in India, the earliest Indian journal of anthropology; Ghurye later founded Sociological Bulletin.

qa.q: How did Sarat Chandra Roy come to anthropology?
qa.a: Through his work as a lawyer and court interpreter in tribal cases
qa.e: His legal work required understanding tribal customs.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Colonial administrators carried out ethnographic surveys and censuses.
Reason (R): Knowledge about the population helped the colonial state govern.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; administrative needs motivated the surveys.

qa.q: Which of these was a British administrator-anthropologist?
qa.a: Edgar Thurston
qa.e: Thurston, like Risley and Hutton, was a colonial official.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Both Iyer and Roy were formally trained anthropologists from the start.
Reason (R): Many early Indian anthropologists entered the field by accident.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false; R is true and describes how they actually began.

qa.q: Ghurye is regarded as the founder of:
qa.a: Institutionalised sociology in India
qa.e: He built the department, society and journal.

qa.q: Ghurye founded which journal?
qa.a: Sociological Bulletin
qa.e: It is the journal of the Indian Sociological Society.

qa.q: Ghurye's Ph.D. thesis was published as:
qa.a: Caste and Race in India
qa.e: Published in 1932.

qa.q: For how many years did Ghurye head the Bombay department?
qa.e: He headed it from 1924 to 1959, i.e. 35 years.

qa.q: Diffusionism is the idea that:
qa.a: Cultural traits spread from one culture to others
qa.e: Diffusionists traced the spread of traits.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Ghurye studied under W.H.R. Rivers at Cambridge.
Reason (R): Diffusionism was one of the influences on Ghurye's work.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true; R describes an influence but does not explain why he studied under Rivers.

qa.q: Which was NOT an influence on Ghurye's work?
qa.a: Weber's theory of bureaucracy
qa.e: The chapter lists diffusionism, Orientalism and nationalism.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Ghurye headed the sociology department at Bombay University for 35 years.
Reason (R): Ghurye is regarded as the founder of institutionalised sociology in India.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; R is a consequence-style judgement, not the explanation of his long headship.

qa.q: The protectionist view in the tribe debate held that:
qa.a: Tribes needed protection and should be kept relatively separate
qa.e: Protectionists feared exploitation and cultural loss.

qa.q: Ghurye described India's tribes as:
qa.a: 'Backward Hindus'
qa.e: He saw them as part of Hindu society, further behind in assimilation.

qa.q: Nationalists criticised British protectionism because they saw it as:
qa.a: A way to keep tribes apart and divide Indians
qa.e: They suspected divide-and-rule motives.

qa.q: Who is best known as a voice of the protectionist position?
qa.a: Verrier Elwin
qa.e: Elwin argued for protecting tribal communities.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Ghurye argued that tribes should be integrated into Hindu society.
Reason (R): Ghurye believed tribes had long interacted with Hindu society.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; long interaction is why he saw integration as natural.

qa.q: Which current issue connects to the tribe debate?
qa.a: Displacement of tribes by dams and mines
qa.e: Development projects raise the same protection-versus-integration questions.

qa.q: Case: A government plans a large dam that would submerge tribal villages, promising jobs in return. A protectionist would most likely stress:
qa.a: The risk of exploitation and cultural loss for the tribes
qa.e: Protectionists emphasised vulnerability to outside exploitation.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Protectionists believed contact with outsiders would benefit tribes greatly.
Reason (R): Protectionists feared exploitation by traders and moneylenders.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false; R is true and contradicts A.

qa.q: Risley argued that caste originated in:
qa.a: Race
qa.e: He linked caste to racial origins using body measurements.

qa.q: Anthropometry is:
qa.a: The measurement of the human body
qa.e: Risley measured features like nose width.

qa.q: According to Risley, upper castes were of:
qa.a: Aryan origin
qa.e: He claimed upper castes were Aryan.

qa.q: Ghurye's main criticism of Risley was that the racial theory:
qa.a: Applied broadly only to north India
qa.e: Elsewhere differences between castes were small.

qa.q: Ghurye's point about averages was that:
qa.a: Caste-wise averages can hide wide variation within a caste
qa.e: Averages mask internal differences.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Outside north India, anthropometric differences between castes were small.
Reason (R): Different groups had been mixing over long periods.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; long mixing explains the small differences.

qa.q: Case: A survey shows that people of a 'high' and a 'low' caste in a south Indian district have nearly identical average body measurements. This supports:
qa.a: Ghurye's critique of Risley
qa.e: Small differences outside north India undermine the racial thesis.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Ghurye completely rejected all use of anthropometric data.
Reason (R): Ghurye argued that Risley's thesis was only partially correct.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: he engaged with the data and qualified the thesis. R is true.

qa.q: How many features of caste did Ghurye identify?
qa.e: Ghurye listed six features.

qa.q: Segmental division means that:
qa.a: Society is divided into closed, birth-based segments
qa.e: Membership in a caste segment is fixed by birth.

qa.q: Restrictions on social interaction in Ghurye's list mainly concern:
qa.a: Sharing food, by purity rules
qa.e: Food rules were central.

qa.q: Which is one of Ghurye's six features?
qa.a: Restricted choice of occupation
qa.e: Occupations were traditionally hereditary.

qa.q: Ghurye's restriction on marriage refers mainly to:
qa.a: Caste endogamy
qa.e: Marriage was restricted to within the caste.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Hierarchy is one of Ghurye's features of caste.
Reason (R): Castes were ranked from 'pure' to 'impure'.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; the ranking is what hierarchy means here.

qa.q: 'Laissez-faire' means:
qa.a: Minimal state interference in the economy
qa.e: It is a glossary term linked to Desai's discussion of the state.

qa.q: Case: In an old village record, members of one caste could not enter certain streets or wear certain clothes. Which feature is this?
qa.a: Differential rights and duties
qa.e: Different castes had different rights, e.g. over dress and residence.

qa.q: D.P. Mukerji was associated with which university?
qa.a: Lucknow
qa.e: He taught at Lucknow and belonged to the Lucknow school.

qa.q: The Lucknow school included D.P. Mukerji and:
qa.a: Radhakamal Mukerjee and D.N. Majumdar
qa.e: These three are the Lucknow school's best-known figures.

qa.q: Mukerji's concept of 'living tradition' means a tradition that:
qa.a: Keeps links with the past while adapting to the new
